Islah denies organisational ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, and 26 of the 94 defendants were acquitted.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in the UAE at 6.5 out of 10. For people elsewhere, this means a UN climate summit was chaired by the head of a state oil company preparing oil deals, and crime groups can use Dubai companies to employ the people who pay officials in their own countries.

Uzbekistan.d:
In Uzbekistan, foreign companies have entered valuable state business by paying people on the inside, from the president's family down to staff at state companies. Three foreign telecom groups paid companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, elder daughter of then-President Islam Karimov, to obtain mobile licences and radio frequencies; Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at $869 million, and the three firms later paid about $2.6 billion between them to settle foreign bribery cases. Karimova has been convicted twice in Uzbekistan and remains in prison.

The same habit shows lower down, in the state's oil and rail companies. A steel pipe supplier agreed US penalties after using an agent, whom it expected to pass on money to employees of a state oil and gas producer, to see rival bids and undercut them in four tenders. A French rail engineer settled in France in 2021 after investigators found it had paid nearly $576,000 into an account owned by an official at the national railway, in a tender that a Japanese complaint said was rigged.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 3.8, so the conditions that made such deals possible have not gone away.

For people in Uzbekistan, this meant paying for mobile services whose licences were sold privately to the president's daughter rather than to the operator offering the best terms, and for rail and oil work awarded through bought tenders. Most of the telecom settlement money went to the governments of the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden, not to Uzbekistan, and weak courts leave citizens little means to find out whether officials are making similar arrangements today.

Vietnam.d:
In Vietnam, the documented pattern is businesses and criminal networks buying the officials who are meant to regulate, police or buy from them, from provincial party chiefs up to ministers, senior police chiefs and the central bank.

The largest case is in banking. A property tycoon secretly controlled a commercial bank for a decade through nominee shareholders, used it to take about US$12.5 billion in loans for her own companies, and paid the head of the central bank's inspection department $5.2 million to keep it off the watch list; she was sentenced to death in 2024.

Most cases are about public money. Construction, property and medical-equipment companies have paid provincial party leaders and project boards to rig tenders for roads, bridges and hospital supplies. During the pandemic, businesses paid officials in three ministries to approve the repatriation flights that were the only way home for Vietnamese abroad. The reach goes to the cabinet: two communications ministers were jailed after a state phone company bought a private pay-TV firm at a price AP reported as inflated almost ten times. US settlements describe foreign firms working the same way, through agents and slush funds around state refineries and telecoms customers. Two senior police chiefs were jailed for covering for an online gambling ring, and drug-team officers were convicted of shielding a Laos–Vietnam trafficking network.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.8. For people in Vietnam this means bank savings, hospital budgets, road contracts and even a seat on a flight home have been for sale to whoever paid the official in charge, and officers meant to enforce gambling and drug laws have been convicted of protecting those breaking them.

Albania.d:
Albanian crime groups move cannabis across the sea to Italy and Greece and buy cocaine in Latin America for sale across Europe, and to keep that trade running they reach into the institutions meant to stop it. The record points above all at the police. Since 2023 SPAK, Albania's special anti-corruption prosecutor, has used messages from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service read by European police, to bring case after case in which a former Tirana police chief, provincial police crime chiefs, a border police head, judges and a prosecutor are accused of working for trafficking groups. The accusations are of warning groups about anti-drug operations, leaking data from the national border database, and suppressing charges or cutting sentences for money. These cases have not reached a verdict in the record here, so they remain allegations.

Higher up, Italian police arrested a cousin of the interior minister in a cannabis probe, and wiretaps mentioned the minister. He was convicted only of abuse of office, so no court has found that the group had him working for it.

SPAK has sent the mayor of Tirana, the capital, to trial on charges that four businessmen gave him and his wife more than €1 million in benefits while he approved construction permits; he denies it. It also suspects that at least 19 tenders at the state IT agency were written for chosen contractors, whose firms gained access to police and prison security systems.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Albania 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 5 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, if these charges hold, the officer checking a car or investigating a killing may be passing information to the group responsible.

Antigua and Barbuda.d:
Antigua and Barbuda is a small state with a small civil service, and the documented cases show outsiders with far more money than its government reaching the one official whose signature they needed.

Agents working for Colombia's Medellín Cartel ordered Israeli military weapons in Antigua's name, with forged papers, to arm the forces of a cartel leader. An Israeli diplomatic note said the guns were shipped at the apparent instruction of the minister Vere Bird Jr, son of the prime minister, and after Colombia complained an official inquiry recommended he be barred from public office for life. The island's business as an offshore financial centre, where foreign-run banks take deposits from around the world under Antiguan licences, created the second opening. R. Allen Stanford ran Stanford International Bank from Antigua and was later convicted in the United States of a $7 billion fraud; the head of the Antiguan regulator meant to supervise his bank took cash, private-jet flights and sports tickets from him, left the bank's real assets unexamined and told US investigators his office had no power to help them.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores the country 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4.7 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, both cases meant outsiders used the state's name and licences for their own business: Antigua's name went on a cartel's arms order, and thousands of savers, on the island and abroad, lost their money in a bank that the regulator had been paid not to look at. In both cases the facts came out through pressure from abroad, from Colombia and from US prosecutors, rather than from Antigua's own institutions.

Austria.d:
Austria sits between east and west, and Vienna has long been a base for foreign spy services. The documented reach-in runs mostly from Russia, into Austria's own security state and into international bodies based here, and it lasts decades. An Austrian army colonel passed military secrets to the GRU, Russia's military intelligence, from 1992 until 2018 for about €280,000, and was convicted in 2020.

The same reach has since appeared inside Austria's domestic intelligence agency, through more than one person there. A former officer was convicted in 2026 of working for Russia through Jan Marsalek, the fugitive former Wirecard executive: he used police databases to find people Moscow wanted, including a journalist, and plans to appeal. Prosecutors allege that the agency's former operations chief passed that officer orders from Marsalek and Russian operatives; he fled to Dubai and has not been tried. Russian money has also reached sport: an inquiry found that the president of the Salzburg-based International Biathlon Union took Russian cash and favours for years and shielded Russian athletes from doping action.

Domestic business uses the same route into state companies: prosecutors charge that a large gambling firm helped place a party loyalist in the boardroom of the state-owned casino operator, expecting gambling law to be changed in its favour. The case has not been tried.

For exiles and journalists Russia's government wants to find, the risk is that an official with access to state databases works for a foreign service and can use those records to locate them. For Austrians, officers in the army and the intelligence service have worked for a foreign power while holding secrets the country shares with its EU partners, a state-owned company may have had its managers chosen by a competitor, and the cases surface years after the fact.

Bangladesh.d:
In Bangladesh outsiders have reached public institutions from several directions: business groups taking over banks, a governing party reaching into the body that runs elections, an Islamist movement reaching into the army, and party networks filling the universities.

The banks are where the most money has moved. Under Sheikh Hasina's government, which fell in August 2024, conglomerates close to it came to control lenders holding ordinary people's deposits. From 2017 the S. Alam Group took over Islami Bank Bangladesh and several other Islamic banks, installing its own chairman, board and managers, and holding one bank's shares beyond the legal limit. Media reported huge loans to the group, which the bank denied; the group denies wrongdoing and investigations are open.

Since Hasina's fall, investigators have turned to the elections her party won. The former chief election commissioner was arrested in 2025 over the 2018 vote, in a case alleging that the governing party controlled the officials heading the commission and that they then had the count fixed in its favour; nothing has been proved and he has not been tried. A coup attempt by serving and retired army officers, which the army says it stopped in 2012, was linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned movement seeking a single Islamic state. Since 2024 the interim government has filled the universities from the networks of the BNP and the Islamist Jamaat-e-Islami: 30 of 47 new vice-chancellors had close ties to their teachers' groups.

Foreign suppliers have reached in too. A French secure-document maker settled in France over the Election Commission's 2014 contract for national identity cards, the convention describing an adviser to the prime minister under whose control the award committee acted and who pushed the order from 70 to 90 million cards, with 730,000 euros paid against a false training invoice. A Chinese state-backed contractor sent about 5 million taka to the secretary running the roads division while bidding was open on a highway; he reported it, the money went back to the embassy and the firm was blacklisted. For depositors, the bank holding their savings may have been run for the group that took it over. Prosecutors now allege that the body counting their ballots answered to the party on them, soldiers were drawn into a plot for a movement outside the state, and university leadership has gone to the networks of the parties close to government.

Belize.d:
One case in Belize meets the map's test, and the finding came from abroad. On 15 November 2022 the US State Department barred John Saldivar, national security minister until November 2020, and his immediate family from the United States, saying it had credible information that he accepted bribes in exchange for improperly facilitating the acquisition of Belizean immigration documents, and that he misused a US-donated Coast Guard boat. The release names nobody who paid. Separately, at a US fuel-fraud trial in February 2020, a cooperating witness testified that the financier Lev Dermen handed Saldivar US$25,000 in Miami; Dermen was later sentenced to 40 years. Saldivar says he is innocent, denies any part in immigration corruption, and says the Miami money was campaign finance he spent on sports projects in his constituency.

Belize sits between Mexico and Guatemala on the Caribbean coast, on routes used to move cocaine north from South America, and it offers offshore company registration. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Belize 5.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, in the middle of the range, but only about 3.6 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

The one case fits that picture. What a buyer gets in Belize is paperwork: the right to be a Belizean on paper, or to own a company whose owner is not published. No Belizean court has tried the allegation against Saldivar; what exists is an American visa ban and testimony given in an American courtroom about a different crime. The records that would show more are the ownership of registered companies and how immigration documents are issued and audited.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.d:
Bosnia and Herzegovina sits on the Balkan route by which cocaine reaches western Europe, and the documented pattern today is criminal networks getting people inside the bodies meant to stop them. Messages on Sky and Anom, encrypted phones used by criminals, led prosecutors to contacts in the police and courts: by early 2023 more than 100 suspects had been detained, among them 14 from law enforcement and a judge. Europol, the EU police agency, said arrests in Sarajevo in 2024 included officials working for a cocaine boss's inner circle.

The accusations now reach the commanders and the senior posts. In 2024 investigators detained the head of the federation's special police unit and the acting head of its police directorate in a drug and money-laundering inquiry, with their officers accused of guarding the leader of the Tito and Dino cartel. The United States has said the head of the state intelligence service worked with criminal networks, and that a senior state prosecutor helped hide evidence for drug traffickers; a Bosnian disciplinary body demoted her for abusing her office. These are designations, detentions and charges, with no verdict reported.

During and just after the 1992-95 war, Iran, a wartime ally, built a presence inside the Interior Ministry. The divided government left by the 1995 peace deal, with separate police and ministries in each part of the country, gives outsiders many offices to approach.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bosnia 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 3.9 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, the prosecutor or judge handling their case may be suspected of working for the people they are meant to try, and the squad sent to make an arrest may have been guarding the man they are after.

Bulgaria.d:
Bulgaria sits on the Balkan route, the main land route by which drugs and smuggled goods enter the European Union, and smugglers get through it by paying the customs officers and border police who are supposed to stop them. The United States sanctioned Bulgarian officials and business figures in 2021, its largest such action against any single country, and several of those named held customs and border posts.

The same reach runs into the offices meant to police business and bring charges. The US Treasury said Delyan Peevski, a member of parliament and media owner, used bribes and influence to control key institutions; in 2013 parliament made him head of the national security agency and he quit a day later after mass protests. Prosecutors have charged the inspection chief and a member of the state gambling commission with belonging to the criminal group of the country's largest gambling operator, so the body policing him is alleged to have answered to him, and a serving prosecutor was arrested as part of another crime group. Claims are also under investigation that compromising files on judges and prosecutors were used to steer their decisions.

Russian intelligence is accused of reaching the bodies that guard this NATO member's secrets. Prosecutors charged a ring in 2021 inside the defence ministry, military intelligence and parliament's classified registry with passing NATO and EU documents to Russian military intelligence, and have since accused a reserve general and two senior officers of the counter-intelligence agency meant to stop such spying of working for Moscow. None of it has been settled in court.

For people here, this means goods crossing the border unchecked, regulators and prosecutors who may be working for the people they are meant to investigate, and allied secrets held by officials who may answer to Russia.

Cambodia.d:
One case in Cambodia is on this map, and it is an allegation that both governments reject. The US Treasury says a Chinese state-owned company, Union Development Group, obtained a 99-year lease in 2008 on the Dara Sakor project, almost 20 per cent of the country's coastline, by forming a local company as leaseholder. It says the army used violence to help clear the land and that a senior general and former armed forces chief of staff benefited financially. Treasury imposed sanctions, while a ruling-party spokesman said the state development council had reviewed and approved the plan. If the allegation is right, a foreign company had the use of Cambodian troops, and the people cleared from that land faced soldiers working in its interest.

Beyond this case the entry remains an estimate. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cambodia among the worst countries in the world for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs to push back. US and British sanctions have named political protection as the reason scam compounds, fenced sites where trafficked workers are forced to run online fraud, can operate in the open. On those scores it is likely that criminal money reaches officials, but the record so far shows owners close to power rather than decisions shown to have been taken inside the state for them. Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of the people sanctioned abroad.

Chad.d:
In Chad outside money reaches in at two levels: foreign oil companies seeking rights go to the presidency and the diplomatic service, and drug traffickers go to the security services. Two cases from the oil side have ended in court abroad. An envoy working for CEFC China Energy, which promoted China's Belt and Road programme, offered President Idriss Déby a $2 million bribe, dressed up as a donation, to win oil rights, and was convicted for it in New York in 2018; the company's chairman denied authorising him. Griffiths Energy, a Canadian company, pleaded guilty in 2013 after paying a $2 million fee to a firm controlled by the wife of Chad's ambassador in North America while seeking an oil contract. The ambassador, his wife and his deputy face US charges that remain unproven.

Lower down, tramadol, a prescription painkiller, is trafficked illegally across the Sahel, and the network moving it through Chad counted high-ranking security and intelligence officials among its members. Analysts who read the court papers when ten people were convicted in 2020 described large sums circulating among them, some used in attempts to bribe judges and the security services.

When intelligence officers are inside a trafficking network, Chadians depend for protection on police and courts that the same network has tried to buy, and when oil rights are sought through payments to the president's circle and the country's diplomats, decisions about the main national resource are made for the payer. The 2020 conviction shows Chad's courts can act, but the oil cases were brought in the United States and Canada. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Chad among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest.

Comoros.d:
Comoros, a small island state off East Africa, has been reached by outsiders through the men around its president and through its officials. For about eleven years from 1978, its presidential guard was commanded by Bob Denard, a French mercenary who worked for France's secret services: he led the coup that returned President Ahmed Abdallah to power, then ran the force meant to protect him while building up business interests and Comorian citizenship. When Abdallah ordered the guard disarmed in 1989 he was shot dead shortly afterwards, and Denard led another coup in 1995 that French troops ended; the court that later tried him recognised the secret services' role.

The more recent documented reach comes from a tobacco company. Leaked records from British American Tobacco (BAT) show the company arranging bribes for Comorian officials, part of a run of payments in several African countries that included efforts to block tobacco-control laws based on the World Health Organization's tobacco treaty. A British fraud inquiry closed without charges and BAT denies wrongdoing.

For Comorians, this means that for a decade the armed men around their head of state answered to a foreigner tied to another country's spy service, and if the tobacco payments worked as reported, they now live under weaker limits on tobacco sales and advertising than the treaty sets. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Comoros high for officials working for criminal interests, with very weak courts, police and watchdogs.

Cote d'Ivoire.d:
Two cases are documented in Côte d'Ivoire, and they reach in from opposite directions: an international lender placing its own former official at the head of the economy, and a cocaine network with the criminal police chief of the main port on its side.

In 1990 the International Monetary Fund pressed President Félix Houphouët-Boigny to put Alassane Ouattara, who had directed the IMF's African Department, in charge of economic policy; he became prime minister that November while the IMF's programme was still running, later returned to the IMF as its deputy head, and has been president since 2011. For Ivorians this meant that the man running their economy during an IMF programme came from the lender setting its conditions, and the decisions on spending and prices taken under that programme were made by the lender's own former official.

In April 2022, after a seizure of more than two tonnes of cocaine in Abidjan and San-Pédro, Karamoko Dosso, former commissaire of the criminal police in the port city of San-Pédro, was among nineteen people convicted of drug trafficking and criminal association. The Abidjan appeal court confirmed ten-year sentences for five of those who appealed, including a former Spanish police officer described as the network's organiser, and reduced five others, Dosso's among them, to five years. The officer who ran criminal investigations in the port was working with the network the port's police were meant to stop.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Côte d'Ivoire high for officials working for criminal interests, with courts, police and watchdogs of middling strength.

Czech Republic.d:
The documented outside reach into the Czech state comes from two sides: Russian intelligence, and a lobbyist's network inside public companies. Russia's foreign intelligence service, the SVR, has worked the old way, by recruiting insiders: in 2022 the government confirmed that a long-serving Foreign Ministry employee with top-secret clearance, who had worked at headquarters and in embassies, had repeatedly taken its money for diplomatic information. He was removed, but prosecution was thought unlikely because intelligence material cannot be used in Czech courts. Prague has also been a base for Russian money aimed at legislatures elsewhere: in 2024 the government exposed Voice of Europe, a Russian-funded website that Czech intelligence says passed money to sitting and aspiring European legislators.

At home, police say a group around Michal Redl, a Zlín businessman and lobbyist linked to the STAN party, steered contracts and money at Prague's city-owned transport company, which runs the metro, trams and buses, through a deputy mayor and senior managers of the firm, to benefit businessmen connected to the group, and reached contracts at the state health insurer as well. Thirteen people were charged in 2022, the education minister resigned over his contacts with Redl, and the trial is under way, with the main accused denying guilt.

For Czechs, this means a diplomatic service in which a foreign spy agency was able to pay a cleared official for years, with no trial to show what he passed on, and a city transport company whose contracts, prosecutors say, were decided for a lobbyist's friends rather than for the people who ride it. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Czech officials low to middling for working with criminal interests, with relatively strong institutions.

Dominican Republic.d:
In the Dominican Republic outside money reaches officials through firms seeking state business and, far more often, through the drug trade. Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, admitted paying $92 million in bribes here to win public works, and a former public works minister was convicted over it; Embraer, the Brazilian aircraft maker, admitted promising $3.5 million to an official to sell military aircraft, and the acquittal of a retired colonel and a former defence minister, who deny any bribe, is now subject to a fresh trial. The pattern reaches smaller contractors too: in 2026 prosecutors charged a guarding company with paying the security directors and officers at state utilities and agencies who oversaw its own contracts.

The country is a transit point for cocaine bound for Puerto Rico, the United States and Europe, and traffickers seek protection wherever a shipment can be stopped. Officers of the National Drug Control Agency have been arrested while guarding loads, a navy officer in charge of port security has been accused of moving cocaine, army colonels have been arrested on suspicion of leaking warrants and raid plans, and a fugitive trafficker held a state intelligence card and official gun permits. A congressman and a state agency head were among one cocaine network's contacts, and since 2009 the drug agency has removed hundreds of staff and the police well over a thousand officers.

For Dominicans, public works, military purchases and even the guarding of state buildings have been bought under deals carrying bribes, and the people meant to stop the drug trade have included some accused of working for it. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs.

Equatorial Guinea.d:
Equatorial Guinea is a small oil and gas producer on the Gulf of Guinea, ruled by Teodoro Obiang since 1979, and the record of outsiders reaching into its government runs almost entirely through oil. The foreign companies that produce and trade its oil have paid the president, his family and the officials who award contracts. A 2004 US Senate inquiry found that American oil companies producing most of the country's offshore oil made payments to Obiang, his relatives and officials for land, office leases, security and scholarships for officials' children, and that Obiang and his family held secret shares in their joint ventures with the government. Later, the Dutch company SBM Offshore admitted that between 2008 and 2012 its local agents passed money on to at least nine officials of the oil ministry and the state oil company, and a Swiss-based commodity trader has pleaded guilty in Britain to bribing officials in five African oil states, this one among them.

A French engineering group settled in 2023 over $2m paid to a partner with privileged access to the president's son, then secretary of state for mines and hydrocarbons, around work for a consortium including the state oil company; the prosecutor says the money was meant for him, not that it arrived. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 9 out of 10, among the highest anywhere, and the courts, police and watchdogs that would resist them at just over 2. That combination describes a state where the people in office control the main source of money and no independent body can question how contracts are given out.

For Equatoguineans, this means oil revenue that could pay for services has been shared between foreign companies and the ruling family, with officials' children educated abroad on company money. With one president in power for more than four decades and weak courts, they have no domestic route to find out who was paid; every documented case was brought by investigators abroad.

Ethiopia.d:
Ethiopia's documented case is in fuel. Prosecutors charged fuel traders along with the deputy director general of the Petroleum and Energy Authority, the body that issues the permits the trade depends on, saying the traders worked through the officials who grant them so that the regulator's own decisions went their way. The case is at indictment, not conviction, and nobody has been found guilty.

That is the shape of the problem where it has been documented: not an outside group placing its people in office, but companies paying the officials inside a regulator so that permits, licences and the rules applied to them come out as they want.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 6 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at 4.5, which suggests more is going on than has been documented. Civil war in Tigray and continuing conflict in Amhara and Oromia make reporting on officials harder, and the weak watchdogs mean there is little official scrutiny of how decisions are made.

For Ethiopians this means the price and supply of fuel, which moves the cost of everything else they buy, has been decided in part by officials the traders were paying, and that a charge brought is not the same as a case concluded.

Gabon.d:
Two accounts sit on the record in Gabon. The first concerns the forest. A Chinese timber group is reported to have paid Gabonese ministers, the people who hand out logging concessions, so that its concessions were granted and then left unchecked; the same report describes payments to ministers in the neighbouring Republic of Congo. It rests on reporting rather than a court ruling, no one has been charged, and it stands as an allegation.

The second is a court record rather than reporting: a Gabonese company settled with the Paris prosecutor in 2024 over its work as local representative for a French maker of military uniforms, which won a 2005 contract worth 7.5 million euros to supply Gabon's security forces. The prosecutor identified an economic and financial affairs adviser in the defence minister's office, who held the power to commit spending, as likely to have received undue advantages. These two accounts sit alongside what the broader measures suggest. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for outside or criminal interests in Gabon at 7.5 out of 10, and the courts and watchdogs that should catch them at 3.5. In a state scoring that way an official can work for an outside buyer with little risk of being exposed, which also means the thinness of the record may say more about how little is investigated than about how little happens.

For Gabonese the practical effect is that the forest is allocated by ministers who, on this account, were being paid by one of the companies bidding for it, and there is no court or auditor at home that has tested the claim. What is known came from outside the country.

Ghana.d:
Ghana's record holds four cases: traffickers reaching a senior police officer, a banker accused of moving a client's money to politicians, a contested case of a foreign company working through a politician's relative, and a French engineering group's payments around the state oil company. Cocaine moves through West Africa on its way to Europe and the United States, and the traffickers who move it need officials who will look away.

In 2006 a large cocaine load landed from a ship and then disappeared. Traffickers were secretly taped meeting the police director of operations at his home about their missing drugs. An inquiry found the police account unsatisfactory and recommended that he be prosecuted, but he was later recalled to duty.

The other two cases are companies buying decisions. US regulators said a banker channelled about $2.5 million from a Turkish energy company to Ghanaian members of parliament and officials who had to approve the power plant it wanted to build; he settled without the allegations being tried. UK court papers said Airbus hired a close relative of a high-ranking elected official as its business partner while selling military transport planes to Ghana, and Airbus's 2020 settlement with France, Britain and the United States included failure to prevent bribery there; in 2024 Ghana's Special Prosecutor closed its own inquiry, finding no evidence that the official took bribes.

For Ghanaians, a senior officer in the force meant to stop the drug trade was reached by traffickers and returned to duty despite the inquiry's recommendation, and the approval of a power station they pay for is alleged to have been bought from their own legislators. A French engineering group settled with France's financial prosecutor in 2023 over a commercial partner paid about 1 per cent of two contracts in which the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation sat on the client side; the convention says part of that money was likely passed on to GNPC executives, one of whom took part in awarding the work. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5.3. Four cases cannot show how common any of this is.

Guinea.d:
Guinea holds one of the world's largest untapped iron ore deposits, at Simandou. The documented cases of outside interests getting inside its government are about who controls its minerals, and they run from foreign companies to the president's household and the minister in charge of mines.

In 2008 the government took two blocks of Simandou from one mining company and gave them to a company controlled by Israeli businessman Beny Steinmetz; a Swiss court later found that he got them by bribing a wife of President Lansana Conté, which he denies. The company that lost the blocks, trying to keep its rights, hired a French banker who was a close friend of a former senior Guinean official, and US regulators found that, acting for it, he offered at least $822,000 to a Guinean official; it paid a $15 million penalty without admitting or denying the findings. Separately, executives of Chinese-linked companies paid mines minister Mahmoud Thiam $8.5 million to become first shareholder in a national mining company that would hold Guinea's stakes, and a New York jury convicted him of laundering the money.

In all three the way to national resources ran through payments to people close to power rather than through open bidding. For Guineans, that meant control of the country's main mineral wealth was fought over through the president's household and the officials who negotiated the terms, and years of potential state revenue were lost while the rights were contested. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 8 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at under 3, so cases like these tend to be pursued abroad, if at all.

Honduras.d:
Honduras is one of the main stopping points for cocaine flown and shipped from South America towards Mexico and the United States, and over two decades trafficking groups bought protection at the top of the state. According to US courts, traffickers paid a president, his brother in Congress and a national police chief to let cocaine through, and trial evidence said drug money paid for the governing National Party's election campaigns. The clearest single case is Juan Orlando Hernández, president from 2014 to 2022, convicted in New York of protecting cocaine shipments and pardoned by the US in 2025.

The police are where the arrangement shows most consistently. Officers who have pleaded guilty in US courts include one who, prosecutors said, led colleagues in escorting tons of cocaine and another who passed police information to the Cachiros, a Honduran trafficking clan, for a decade. Trafficking also worked from the bottom up: on the Guatemalan border, a trafficker became mayor of his own town and, US prosecutors said, paid into the ruling party's presidential campaign in return for protection.

Private money has bought Honduran office-holders in other bodies too. A US uniform maker's chief was convicted in 2025 over bribes for police contracts, and the firms buying football broadcasting rights paid two Hondurans on the selling side, the president of CONCACAF, which runs the game in North and Central America, and the head of the national federation; both admitted it.

For Hondurans, mayors, police, Congress and the presidency have all been used to move cocaine, and the main cases were tried abroad; the former president has been released, though Honduras has an arrest order out for him. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at under 4.

Indonesia.d:
In Indonesia outside forces reach the state mainly through money, business and religious movements. Under Suharto, a Muslim intellectuals' association headed by the minister Habibie moved its members into the civil service and ministries and used that place to set up religious courts and an Islamic bank. Officials say Jemaah Islamiyah, the network behind the 2002 Bali bombings, spent over a decade trying to get its people into the military, police and ministries.

Business helps write the law and decide how it is applied. When the government drafted its 2020 omnibus law, which rewrote dozens of laws on labour, land and permits, the chairman of the national chamber of commerce ran the consultation. Firms have paid the people who buy from them, judge them or guard state assets: aircraft makers paid the head of the state airline, power-plant bidders paid MPs and the head of the state electricity company, a German software maker's agents paid officials in a ministry and a state telecoms agency that then bought its products, and prosecutors say palm-oil groups' lawyers paid judges to acquit them. At the state tin company, directors let private smelters mine its concessions under a disguised lease, at a cost put at about 300 trillion rupiah.

The reach now extends to the count of the vote: a court convicted a serving member of the election commission, the body that allots parliamentary seats, of taking the governing party's cash and awarding a seat to its man.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Indonesian officials 8 out of 10 for working for criminal interests. For Indonesians, the rules on their wages and land were drafted with employers at the head of the table, and both a court verdict and a seat in parliament can depend on who has paid.

Israel.d:
In Israel the outside party with the deepest reach into the state is the settler movement, which builds settlements in the occupied West Bank and has long drawn state money to outposts the government's own rules forbade. One of the movement's leaders runs the civil administration that rules on land and building there. After the 7 October 2023 attack the movement also came to sit inside the army: thousands of settlers called up as reservists serve in local defence units staffed largely by residents of the settlements they guard, and dozens have been dismissed for attacking Palestinians.

The ultra-Orthodox parties take their decisions from councils of senior rabbis, who used their place in government to protect seminary students' exemption from military service and in 2025 ordered their ministers out when the Supreme Court told the army to draft them.

Prosecutors say Benjamin Netanyahu, as communications minister, gave a telecoms owner valuable decisions in return for favourable coverage, which he denies; a former head of his bureau and a former minister are charged with taking bribes from the agent of a German shipbuilder selling the state submarines. A separate case ended in convictions: five senior managers of the Israel Electric Corporation, the state power company, were jailed in 2017 over about 20 million dollars Siemens paid through a consultant owned by one manager's brother-in-law, around contracts worth some 786 million dollars. Iranian intelligence recruits Israelis for money, and the recruits are now inside the forces: prosecutors have charged soldiers in combat brigades and in the Iron Dome missile-defence system with photographing bases for an Iranian handler, some of them, they say, recruited before they enlisted. By the end of 2025, 35 such espionage cases had been made public.

For Palestinians in the West Bank, the official deciding whether their homes stand comes from the movement that wants their land, and the soldiers posted near their villages are often settlers from nearby. For Israelis, who serves in the army has been set partly in rabbis' councils, and some who serve stand charged with working for Iran.

Jordan.d:
In Jordan, outside forces have reached the state through its rulers, its border guards and its parliament. For about twenty years, until 1977, the CIA made secret yearly payments of millions of dollars to King Hussein; President Carter stopped them just before The Washington Post reported them. Today's pressure comes from drug smugglers on the Syrian border. Smugglers moving captagon, an amphetamine pill made in Syria, need the border to stay open to them, so they recruit the people guarding it, and serving and former soldiers have been convicted of carrying pills and weapons across.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement that works to bring its members into power, competed openly through its own party, the Islamic Action Front, which became the largest party in parliament in the 2024 election. In 2025 the government banned all of the Brotherhood's activities and said it would seize its assets, after arrests over an alleged weapons plot that the group said it knew nothing about.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Jordan 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and above 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For families in northern Jordan this means living on a smuggling route where some of the soldiers paid to stop the drugs have been caught moving them. For the voters who made the Islamic Action Front the largest party, it means their party's parent movement is now banned and its members face arrest.

Korea, DPR.d:
In North Korea the state itself is the organisation that crosses borders, and the one documented case on this map runs the other way: the government reaching into an international body rather than an outside force reaching into it. In the Pyongyang office of the UN Development Programme, the UN's main aid agency, most local staff were nominees chosen by the government against UN policy, their salaries were paid to the state in hard currency, officials had to be present at project visits, and the government moved its own funds abroad through a UN account. A 2008 US Senate inquiry set this out, and the UN suspended its programme there in 2007 after the government refused new controls.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives North Korea the worst possible score, 10 out of 10, for officials taking part in criminal activity, and one of the lowest anywhere for its courts and watchdogs. The US Justice Department has charged networks that placed thousands of North Korean IT workers, using stolen or fake identities, in remote jobs at foreign companies, with their wages paid into accounts controlled by the state.

For people in North Korea this means that aid meant for them passes through staff picked by the government, and money from work done abroad in their name goes to the state rather than to them. With no independent courts, press or watchdogs, they have no means of learning how the aid or the earnings are spent, or of challenging it at home.

Kyrgyzstan.d:
The record in Kyrgyzstan is small and shows money reaching officials at two points: the customs service and the president's circle. Customs decides what crosses the border and what duty is paid on it, so a smuggling operation with people inside controls both what comes in unchecked and how much revenue the state loses. The clearest case is Raiymbek Matraimov, a deputy head of customs whom journalists tied to a scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country, and whom the US sanctioned in 2020; at home he settled by repaying money and served no prison term at the time.

Foreign companies have also gone to the top. US regulators say a global tobacco trader paid more than $3 million in bribes from as early as 1996 so that its local subsidiary could buy Kyrgyz tobacco, most of it delivered in bags of $100 bills to a high-ranking official; the company settled. After the president was ousted in 2010, officials of the new government said the firm supplying jet fuel to the US air base at Manas had paid his son. That remains an allegation, and these records do not show what a US congressional inquiry found.

Journalists from OCCRP, an organised-crime reporting network, and the Kyrgyz outlet Kloop, who documented the customs scheme, were prosecuted or forced out while the official they wrote about stayed free. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kyrgyzstan 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Kyrgyzstan this means customs revenue that should have paid for schools, roads and hospitals has left the country, and the officials at the centre of it have faced little at home.

Lesotho.d:
Lesotho's largest public project is the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, a World Bank-backed scheme of dams and tunnels that sells the country's water to South Africa, and it is where foreign companies reached in most clearly. Engineering and construction firms from abroad paid Masupha Sole, chief executive of the state authority that ran it, through intermediaries, and Swiss bank records later showed millions of maloti he could not explain. In 2002 Lesotho's own High Court convicted him of bribery and it went on to convict a Canadian engineering firm and a German consultancy. A small, poor country prosecuted the foreign companies itself, which is unusual.

Two later matters are less settled. Prosecutors allege that the head of the German company Frazer Solar and a former minister forged a solar deal after Cabinet declined to approve it; the minister says his signature was forged, no bribe is reported, and the case has been revived on appeal. Even so, the company won an arbitration award of about €50 million and has pursued Lesotho's water royalties to collect it. Separately, the deputy army commander said in 2024 that members of the security agencies escort and associate with famo gangs, rival groups blamed for killings, without naming anyone.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Lesotho 7 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people in Lesotho this means the scheme that sells their main natural resource was run for years by an official taking money from the firms building it, income from that same water has been targeted in a dispute over a contract their courts called unlawful, and the forces meant to stop gang killings are said by their own commander to include people close to the gangs.

Lithuania.d:
Lithuania has faced two kinds of reach-in: Russian and Belarusian intelligence recruiting people with access to its armed forces, air infrastructure and security services, and company money reaching politicians and the officials who award contracts.

Russia's military intelligence, the GRU, and its security service, the FSB, repeatedly try to buy people with access. The Šiauliai air base, which hosts NATO's Baltic air patrols, has been hit repeatedly: a GRU agent working as a military surgeon recruited an air force officer there, and a base worker and an accomplice were convicted of photographing orders and layouts for Russian intelligence. An FSB officer was caught in 2015 trying to recruit presidential guards to plant listening devices. Belarus's military intelligence has recruited an employee of the state air traffic company and two Lithuanians, one of whom joined the Riflemen's Union, a volunteer defence organisation linked to the army, in order to spy.

On the money side, parliament impeached a president in 2004 for granting citizenship by decree to a Russian helicopter businessman who had reportedly funded his campaign. Companies buy decisions as well. The French engineering group Alstom paid officials of a state power station and senior politicians, and won 240 million euros of power contracts; in 2024 the Supreme Court made final the convictions of the Liberal Movement's leader, a Labour MP and an executive of a large business group for bribes paid to get decisions through parliament.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Lithuania's institutions as fairly strong and finds a moderate level of officials serving criminal interests. For Lithuanians this means the soldiers, base staff, volunteers and guards protecting them and the members of parliament voting on their laws have each been targets for payment, and that most of those exposed so far have been convicted in Lithuania's own courts.

Malaysia.d:
In Malaysia outside money and networks have reached the state at the top, in the armed forces and at its borders. Goldman Sachs bankers paid bribes to officials in Malaysia and Abu Dhabi to win the bond business of 1MDB, a state investment fund, and billions were then stolen; Najib Razak, prime minister until 2018, was convicted over more than $1 billion found in his own accounts, and is appealing. His successor, Muhyiddin Yassin, is on trial accused of using his office to help firms win contracts under a Covid-era public works programme while they paid money to his party, which he denies.

Defence buying has drawn similar accusations. French investigators allege that French firms paid kickbacks through a defence minister's adviser to sell submarines, which those charged deny. Anti-corruption investigators suspect a cartel of companies paid army officers to rig tenders, and a former army chief has pleaded not guilty to laundering charges. They also allege a smuggling syndicate paid military officers per run.

Traffickers moving methamphetamine from the Golden Triangle pay narcotics officers to release suspects and resell seized drugs, and the commission has prosecuted such officers repeatedly, mostly in Johor and around Kuala Lumpur. The national police chief said in 2021 that 34 members of the force were suspected of working for a single phone-scam gang, and at the main airport the commission says agents pay immigration officers to wave foreigners through.

Rail building has its own case: the Malaysian arm of a French rail contractor settled in France in 2026 after putting two influential public officials and a member of a royal family on the board and payroll of the vehicle it used to bid for the MRT2 line, and paying companies they held stakes in success fees to extract compensation from the state transport operator. For Malaysians, a public fund meant to pay for development filled a prime minister's accounts and left the country with the debt, public money for defence may have gone on bribes, some officers paid to stop drugs have sold them back onto the street, and fraud victims have reported to a force in which some officers were suspected of working for the fraudsters.

Marshall Islands.d:
The documented outside reach into the Marshall Islands is an attempt by foreign businesspeople to buy a law that would have given them their own territory. Two China-born businesspeople paid members of parliament and other officials over several years to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'special administrative region' on Rongelap Atoll. Both pleaded guilty in the United States, and the US government later barred a former Marshallese president and an MP from entering the country for taking the bribes; the former president denies it.

The scheme shows how a small Pacific state can be approached. A parliament of a few dozen members meant that paying a handful of lawmakers could move a law. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a relatively low level of officials serving outside interests in the Marshall Islands, which fits a country where this was a single scheme rather than a settled arrangement.

For the people of Rongelap this means lawmakers were paid to put their home under a separate set of rules written for the buyers. No one has been charged in the Marshall Islands, so the case was settled in a foreign court, and Marshallese have no ruling of their own on which officials took money.

Micronesia.d:
The record for the Federated States of Micronesia holds one accusation made by its own head of state and one foreign bribery conviction. In 2023, shortly before leaving office, President David Panuelo wrote a long letter saying China was using bribery and threats against Micronesian officials as 'political warfare', with the aim of keeping the Pacific country on Beijing's side, or neutral, if war broke out over Taiwan. China rejected the claims, no court or inquiry has tested them, and no official has been named as taking money.

The proven case is smaller and commercial. US prosecutors said a Hawaii engineering firm gave cash, vehicles, gifts and entertainment to Micronesian officials from 2006 to 2016 to win and keep government contracts worth nearly $8 million. Its owner and a transport department official who oversaw aviation programmes, including airport management, pleaded guilty and were sentenced in the US in 2019.

Both accounts describe a method suited to a small state, where paying or pressing a handful of senior officials can move a large decision, whether that is a contract or which of China or Taiwan the country recognises. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a relatively low level of officials serving outside interests in Micronesia.

For Micronesians, this means at least one official overseeing public services such as airports took payments from a firm seeking government contracts. If the president's account is also true, some officials have made foreign policy decisions after taking money or giving way to threats from abroad, and because that has not been investigated, people cannot tell which officials, if any, were involved.

Montenegro.d:
In Montenegro, organised crime has had protectors at the top of the state for three decades. In the 1990s, when cigarettes were smuggled across the Adriatic to Italy, Italian anti-mafia prosecutors charged that the state itself protected the trade and indicted the country's leader, Milo Djukanovic, in 2008; immunity kept him from trial, and he went on to lead Montenegro until 2023.

The smuggling has continued, cocaine has joined cigarettes, and the protection is alleged to have reached the justice system. Since Europol, the EU's police agency, passed Montenegro messages from Sky ECC, a cracked encrypted phone service used by criminals, former heads of the Supreme Court, the special prosecution office and the police have been charged with protecting crime groups. Prosecutors say a cigarette group using the free customs zone at the Port of Bar had a former national police director and the port city's criminal police chief passing it information; both have denied such accusations and no verdict has been reported. The clearest case is the former Supreme Court president convicted in 2026 of using her position to shield a smuggling network run by her son.

Foreign governments have been accused of reaching in too. Prosecutors accused two Russian military intelligence officers of plotting with pro-Russian opposition MPs to seize parliament in 2016; a first court convicted them, but a retrial acquitted everyone.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Montenegro widely serving criminal interests. For people there this means the judges, prosecutors and police chiefs they would turn to may have been working for the groups they were meant to pursue, and anyone whose case reached the Supreme Court in those years cannot be sure it was heard fairly. Most of these charges are still unproven.

Namibia.d:
In Namibia, the documented outside reach is through what the state buys and what it hands out, with foreign companies accused of paying people close to the officials in charge. Neither accusation has been proved in court.

Namibia's fish belong to the public, and the government hands out quotas, licences to catch a set amount. In the case known as 'Fishrot', leaked files published in 2019 indicated that Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, had paid people close to the government to obtain horse-mackerel quotas. The fisheries and justice ministers resigned and were arrested with several associates, and they face racketeering, corruption and money-laundering charges under Namibia's organised crime law. Samherji denies paying bribes, and no one has yet been convicted. In an earlier case, prosecutors alleged in 2009 that Nuctech, a Chinese state-owned scanner maker, inflated the price of a deal with the finance ministry to pay millions of dollars in 'commission' to a firm part-owned by a serving public service commissioner. All three accused were found not guilty.

The mechanism alleged is one seen wherever a few officials control who may take a public resource or win a public contract: a foreign company that pays them or their associates gets a share that would otherwise go to local firms or be sold for the public's benefit. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate-to-high level of officials serving outside interests in Namibia and rates its institutions as fairly weak.

For Namibians, if the charges are proved, two ministers sold a public resource to a foreign company, local fishing firms and their workers lost quota they would otherwise have had, and the state lost income for the public budget. The trial has run for years, so people still wait for a court to say who took part.

New Zealand.d:
In New Zealand the documented reach inside government is small and comes from three directions: the Chinese state, which media reports say had people in Parliament whose ties to it were known to the intelligence services but not to voters; drug networks, which police say have paid prison staff; and contractors paying the public managers who buy from them.

The clearest example of the first is Jian Yang, a National MP who had been a Communist Party member and had taught at Chinese army schools that trained intelligence linguists. New Zealand media reported that the agencies had raised concerns about his relationship with the Chinese government; he and a second MP left Parliament at an election. No official finding backs those reports.

Organised crime has generally had little hold on officials, and the Global Organized Crime Index gives New Zealand one of the world's lowest scores on that measure. The exception now before the courts is in Auckland's prisons, where police allege that prisoners coordinating drug imports from their cells had staff take cash to bring in phones and drugs. In 2026 police charged fifteen prison staff, five of them employed by Serco, the private company running one jail. The proven cases are in local government: a road contractor paid more than $1 million over eight years to a senior manager at a local council and then Auckland Transport, and both were jailed.

For New Zealanders, this means they elected MPs whose links to a foreign government were reportedly known to the security services and not to them, some officers paid to keep prisons closed may have been working for the people held inside, and spending on Auckland's roads was for years overseen by a manager taking money from the firm doing the work.

North Macedonia.d:
In North Macedonia outsiders have reached into politics and the justice system by paying or directing individual office-holders, most visibly around the 2018 agreement that renamed the country so it could join NATO, which Russia opposed. Interior ministry documents seen by investigative reporters say Ivan Savvidis, a Russian-Greek billionaire and former member of Russia's parliament for the ruling party, paid at least €300,000, some carried across the Greek border in cash, to more than a dozen politicians from several parties, nationalist groups and football hooligans ahead of protests in which a petrol bomb was thrown at parliament; he denied funding the protests. Leaked counter-intelligence files from 2017 say a Serbian intelligence officer at Serbia's embassy gave instructions to an MP in the ruling coalition and that Russian intelligence officers tried to recruit army and interior ministry staff.

The justice system has been bought from inside as well. The Special Prosecution Office, set up to pursue high-level crime after a wiretapping scandal, was compromised when a television personality close to its head sold the country's richest man milder treatment in his case; in 2020 a court jailed him for bribing her and jailed her for misuse of office. Separately, the foreign minister joined the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders network in 2025, which is lawful and shows no decision taken for it.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives North Macedonia a fairly high score for officials working for criminal or outside interests and middling strength in its courts and watchdogs. For people in North Macedonia this means a decision about their country's name and alliances was contested with foreign money paid to their own politicians, and the office created to prosecute the powerful was itself for sale.

Palau.d:
The record for Palau, a Pacific island country that hosts US airstrips and radar sites, is two allegations rather than any settled finding. Both involve money from Chinese interests reaching a Palauan official who controls something foreign buyers want, the laws or the land, and neither has been tested in a Palauan court.

In February 2026 the US State Department barred Hokkons Baules, president of Palau's Senate, and his family from entering the United States, saying he accepted bribes for supporting 'government, business, and criminal interests from China'. Reuters reported in 2025 that three Palauan officials said Baules phoned a customs officer after a Chinese investor allegedly arrived with $119,000 in undeclared cash; Baules said he did not recall that. He denies wrongdoing, says he was accused because he helped Chinese investors, and says Palau's authorities could charge him if they have evidence. China called Reuters's claims fabricated.

The second account concerns public land. The chairman of a state public land authority, who also served as Speaker of the House of Delegates, is reported to have been paid directly by a Chinese national, and land in his state was leased out without the approvals the law requires. No charge has followed.

For people in Palau, this means the head of one chamber of their legislature and the man who held their state's public land both stand accused of taking money from Chinese interests while deciding matters those interests cared about, and that the accusations have come from a foreign government and foreign reporters, with nothing at home that has tested them either way.

Peru.d:
In Peru, money from builders has reached the presidency and the transport ministry, and criminal networks have bought people inside the offices that keep the country's records, grant its pardons, guard its ports and store its weapons.

Public works are where the money has gone deepest. Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group, paid former president Toledo about $35 million for the contract to build the Interoceanic Highway, and he has been sentenced over it. Peruvian firms have done the same at home: prosecutors say a cartel of construction companies paid transport ministry officials so that 30 public works went to its members, four of the firms have admitted responsibility, and in 2025 another former president, Martín Vizcarra, was convicted of taking money from two builders while a regional governor; he is appealing.

Lower down, staff of the national property registry rewrote the recorded owners of disputed land, officials of the board advising the president on pardons sold early release to traffickers, cocaine groups were reported to pay security staff and dockworkers at Callao, and an army lieutenant is accused of supplying rifle ammunition to Ecuadorian gangs. Police disciplinary records from 2019 to 2024 show 96 officers implicated in 37 cases of helping illegal gold miners, with only six ending in sanctions fully upheld. Unnamed witnesses on television made similar claims about a later national police chief, which he rejects and which are unverified. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Peru high for officials working for criminal interests.

For Peruvians this means they have paid for roads, irrigation and hospitals awarded in return for bribes, a land title has been changed for whoever paid the registrar, traffickers have bought early release, and police have been accused of warning illegal miners of raids.

Qatar.d:
Qatar's documented cases run in two directions: foreign arms makers paying the officials who buy for its armed forces, and Qatar's own money reported to have reached inside another country's government.

The clearest case is in arms buying. The US Justice Department found that Raytheon, the American missile maker now part of RTX, paid at least $2 million from 2012 to 2016 through sham contracts with a company owned by the official who ran procurement for the Qatar Emiri Air Force, and won additions to an air-defence contract in return; RTX agreed in 2024 to pay a $252 million criminal penalty for the bribery. Going the other way, Israeli prosecutors are investigating aides of the Israeli prime minister over money reported to have come from Qatar to promote its image from inside his office.

Qatar's residents have no elected body able to ask how state money is spent, whether on weapons at home or on influence abroad, and the air-force case came to light only through a US prosecution. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Qatar fairly high for officials working for criminal or outside interests.

Samoa.d:
Samoa's two documented cases both involve people paying for the right to cross a border. In 2019 a court jailed an assistant immigration officer who had been paid by buyers abroad to push Samoan passports through for people with no right to them, using the government's own document system. In 2025 a Samoan broker was convicted of paying a contact inside New Zealand's immigration office in Samoa, so that the visa applications he handled were treated favourably and workers entered New Zealand illegally.

Both show the same route into a small administration: one member of staff holds a decision that somebody abroad badly wants, and that person pays the member of staff directly. In both cases the state the officer worked for was not the only one affected, since a Samoan passport and a New Zealand visa are documents other countries rely on.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Samoa in its low band, scoring it low for officials working for criminal or outside interests and in the middle range for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For residents, the courts have shown they will jail an official who sells a document, and the two cases on the record are too few to show how often it happens.

Senegal.d:
In Senegal the one documented claim of an outside group getting inside the state concerns a drug ring and the police. In 2013 the country's anti-drug chief accused his predecessor, by then national police chief, of having worked with a drug ring while he ran the anti-drug office. The police chief was removed, but an inquiry found no evidence, and the claim remains contested.

It does not show a pattern, and no other case on the map shows a foreign state, crime group or company getting its people or money inside a Senegalese public body.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Senegal in the middle range both for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For Senegalese, this means the officials they deal with are rated as neither often nor rarely acting for criminal interests, and the one serious accusation against a police chief was investigated and not upheld.

Singapore.d:
Singapore appears on the map mainly as a base from which other institutions are reached. For years a Singapore ship-supply firm run by Leonard Francis bribed US Navy officers with cash, travel and gifts for ship schedules and inside information, while a civilian Navy contracting officer in Singapore stopped an early inquiry; US prosecutors charged 33 people. Criminal money also works through staff inside the banks here: a relationship manager at Citibank's Singapore branch was convicted in 2025 of opening accounts for a money-laundering syndicate and faking the paperwork the bank used to check its clients, so the checks were defeated from the inside.

At home, the government treats foreign influence, most often linked to China, as something that works through ordinary community life: business chambers, clan and grassroots associations and universities. Its response is to name the people it believes are being used, and it does this by ministerial decision, not by trial. Since 2024 a foreign-interference law lets it designate residents, so far a business-chamber leader who had attended a Chinese Communist Party united front body, and make them report each year their political donations and foreign ties.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 1.5 out of 10, among the lowest in the world, and courts and watchdogs at about 7.8. For residents this means the bribery on record ran through a local firm into a foreign navy and through a bank employee into the financial system rather than into their own government, while people who lead community or business groups with ties to China can be publicly named and made to disclose their links without the evidence being tested in court.

Somalia.d:
In Somalia the outside force reaching furthest into the state is al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked armed Islamist group fighting the federal government, which places its own people inside the government it is trying to overthrow. Its members take public jobs, sometimes under false names, to collect information for taxing businesses and choosing targets, and in 2019 a woman working under a false name in the Mogadishu mayor's office blew herself up at a meeting there, killing the mayor and other officials. In 2023 the national intelligence agency said it had arrested ten al-Shabaab spies inside government agencies in Mogadishu, and opposition parties have urged the president to purge the agency itself.

Its reach extends to the systems that carry money and goods. UN monitors reported that it got inside the institutions running Mogadishu's port and used cargo manifests to tax importers, and that it moved funds through a mobile-money company, two of whose staff were prosecuted over a 2017 truck bomb. Monitors also reported government commanders supplying ammunition that reached the group, and in 2014 alleged that a man they called a presidential adviser steered state weapons to it, which he and the president denied.

Commercial money reaches the ministries. The UN Monitoring Group documented that Soma Oil & Gas, a British company, paid the salaries of fourteen officials of the Ministry of Petroleum, among them the director general, his deputy and a director on the team negotiating Soma's own production-sharing terms, while that negotiation was running; six were drawing their civil service pay at the same time. Two weeks after the terms were agreed the minister widened the area Soma could survey. The Group called it a likely quid pro quo. Britain's Serious Fraud Office investigated and closed the case in December 2016 for insufficient evidence; the company and the minister deny wrongdoing.

Foreign states compete at the top as well: from 2019 to 2021 the intelligence agency was run by a former reporter for Qatar's state-funded Al Jazeera, whom Somali media and analysts accuse of channelling Qatari money and interests into government, which Qatar denies.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 1.9. For people in Somalia that means paying tax twice, to the government and to the group fighting it, and working in offices where a colleague may be passing on who should be taxed or killed.

Sri Lanka.d:
In Sri Lanka three kinds of outside force are documented inside the state: organised crime, which is accused of buying officers in the army and police; foreign companies paying the heads of state enterprises; and a Buddhist nationalist movement, whose leader was given a hand in writing the law.

The crime side came to light in 2025, when the gang leader Kehelbaddara Padme was returned from Indonesia with four associates. Investigators say his network had people across the security forces, with army officers detained over allegedly selling firearms and ammunition to the gang and a police sub-inspector arrested over close ties to him. The public security minister said police and immigration officials helped the gang obtain forged passports.

A UK settlement with Airbus described a US$2 million bribery arrangement through a firm in the name of the wife of the chief executive of SriLankan Airlines during a 2013 aircraft sale. Sri Lanka's bribery commission alleges money went on to the Rajapaksa family; the son it names denies it, and that part is unproven. In 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa put Gnanasara, leader of Bodu Bala Sena ('Buddhist Power Force'), a monks' group accused of stirring violence against Muslims, in charge of a task force to draft a single legal code, work the Bar Association said belonged to Parliament and the Justice Ministry.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.7. For people in Sri Lanka this means guns from army officers and passports obtained with officials' help may have reached a gang, the state airline's aircraft deal involved a bribe, and Muslims and other minorities saw their law being drafted by a cleric whose group was accused of violence against them.

Sudan.d:
In Sudan armed and political movements have repeatedly taken over the state from inside. The longest-running is the Islamist movement derived from the Muslim Brotherhood. Led by Hassan al-Turabi, it spent the decade after he became attorney general in 1979 placing members in high posts, took power through army officers in 1989, and under Omar al-Bashir filled state jobs with its own people. A committee set up after Bashir fell in 2019 began removing them, but after the army's coup of 2021 a special court reinstated scores of officials in the central bank, the judiciary and the ministries.

Since the war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary began in 2023, the Islamists have gone back inside the army itself. Thousands of men from Bashir's former intelligence service are reported to have joined the army, the US says one Islamist brigade has supplied more than 20,000 fighters, and the army chief relies on Islamist backing. Armed Darfur movements entered by another door: a 2020 peace deal gave them about a quarter of the cabinet, and one rebel leader has run the finance ministry since 2021, staffing it with his own members.

The fighting forces have reached into the banking system too. US sanctions documents say front companies tied to the Rapid Support Forces bought a majority stake in a commercial bank, so a licensed bank's accounts carried the money for one side's war.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8.5 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at about 2.3. For people in Sudan, this means the courts, the central bank, the ministries and now a bank holding their money are run by the appointees or owners of fighting movements rather than by people chosen for the job.

Syria.d:
Syria's state was taken over in the 1960s by a closed group that built its own structure first. The Military Committee, a secret body of army officers formed in 1958 and hidden even from their own Ba'ath party's leaders, used army units to carry out the 1963 coup and held the real power inside the new government. One of its founders, Hafez al-Assad, seized power in 1970, and he and his son Bashar ruled until December 2024.

That ruling circle was itself reached from outside. By 1965 Israel's Mossad had planted an agent, Eli Cohen, under a false identity among Syria's leaders, where he heard officials discuss army plans and reported them to Israel.

The Global Organized Crime Index gave Assad's Syria 10 out of 10 for state-embedded crime and about 2 for courts and watchdogs. For people in Syria, this meant decades of rule by a group that had organised in secret inside the army, with police and courts that answered to it rather than to them, and no independent court or elected body able to hold it to account.

Thailand.d:
In Thailand criminal businesses reach into the state mainly through the police, who have been accused of selling protection to gambling, drug and visa rackets. In 2023 the deputy national police chief was removed and investigated over alleged protection of an online gambling network, splitting the police leadership in public.

Chinese crime groups in Thailand have used the same route, and local government too. In a crackdown that began in late 2022, investigators charged at least 80 immigration police, three of them generals, with demanding bribes over visas issued to about 5,000 Chinese nationals, and six officers were dismissed over links to a Chinese businessman whom a court acquitted in 2025 for insufficient evidence. Investigators allege that district chiefs and village headmen took bribes to grant citizenship to Chinese nationals, and a newsletter's claim that scam networks paid a deputy finance minister's wife led to his resignation; he denies it and is suing.

Foreign companies pay for state business through middlemen, and the buying runs through the services as well as the ministries.
