Rolls-Royce's 2017 British settlement described about US$36 million paid to intermediaries, some reaching state airline staff, though a Thai court dismissed the resulting case for weak evidence; in 2024 the American machinery maker Deere settled over payments by its Thai arm to officials of the air force and two roads departments, which then bought its equipment.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime at 7 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5. For people in Thailand, the officer or district chief who decides on a visa, a citizenship paper or a complaint may be working for the businesses involved, and the air force and roads departments bought their equipment from a firm that had paid their own officials.

Trinidad and Tobago.d:
In Trinidad and Tobago the documented reach-in has come through people holding public posts while serving outside interests: contractors on the country's largest public works, an international sports body, and now armed gangs. The clearest case is the new terminal at Piarco International Airport, built in the late 1990s: contractors, led by a Miami engineering firm, worked with the then finance minister to rig bids and charge inflated prices. In 2023 a Miami jury found the former minister and two businessmen liable for racketeering and fraud, awarding the country US$131.3 million. Jack Warner, meanwhile, was a vice-president of FIFA, world football's governing body, while he served as works minister and then national security minister until 2013; US prosecutors later charged him with taking bribes in his football roles, charges never tried because Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition in 2025.

The gangs reach in through the prisons. When the government declared a state of emergency in July 2025 over a plot, hatched by jailed gang leaders, to kill public officials, it detained a prison superintendent it said had used his post to get contraband to the plotters and support the gangs' leaders inside.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores both officials acting for criminal interests and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5 out of 10. For people in Trinidad and Tobago this means the airport they paid for cost far more than it should have because their finance minister was working with the contractors, that the minister once responsible for their police was also an officer of a body later accused of selling votes, and that gang leaders the state has locked up can still plan killings with help from the officers guarding them.

Tuvalu.d:
No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Tuvalu is documented, so this account is an estimate based on conditions. Tuvalu is a nation of about 11,000 people on low-lying atolls, and its government depends heavily on foreign aid and on agreements with larger partners. Elsewhere in the Pacific, payments for business deals have drawn smaller states into larger powers' rivalries; none of this is documented in Tuvalu.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Tuvalu in its Minimal band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 1.5 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at 5.9. For Tuvaluans this means there is no known current harm from hidden outside influence. The risk is that a country this small has only a handful of officials, auditors and police, so if an outside interest did reach in, there would be few people in a position to notice it.

United Kingdom.d:
In Britain outsiders reach in through foreign intelligence services recruiting inside the state, fraternities placing members in office, paramilitary and far-right groups entering the security forces, companies entering the departments that regulate them, and crime groups buying port staff. Soviet intelligence had agents inside MI6, MI5 and the Foreign Office last century; today China and Iran are most active. MI5 says a solicitor working covertly with China's United Front gave donations to an MP.

In Northern Ireland every prime minister from 1921 to 1969 belonged to the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity. Loyalist paramilitaries drew on the security forces for men and information: a 1973 army estimate put up to 15% of a local regiment in loyalist groups, and a government review reported a 1985 MI5 assessment that 85% of the intelligence held by the UDA, a loyalist group, came from security force sources, while finding no overarching state conspiracy. Neo-Nazi National Action tried to grow inside the army, and a serving corporal was convicted of belonging to it. In England, a detective has said Masonic officers took him off an inquiry that pointed to the lodges.

Firms have paid MPs to lobby, the big accountants lend tax staff to the Treasury to help draft law they then advise on, and a Conservative peer pushed her husband's firm through the pandemic contracts 'VIP lane'. At the ports, cocaine importers recruit port security guards and Border Force officers to pass their vans and couriers.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials serving criminal interests at 3 out of 10 and courts at 7.6. For Britons, this means rules drafted or enforced by those they apply to, drugs passing checkpoints staffed by a gang's recruits, and, in Northern Ireland, families still seeking inquiries into killings in which soldiers and police took part.

Vanuatu.d:
Vanuatu's one documented case is small and plain. An importer paid a customs border officer to release her shipping container without inspecting it, and a court convicted them, so the check that would have found the undeclared goods was simply called off. That is the common form this takes in a country whose trade arrives by sea: not an organisation placed inside the government, but one official at the point where goods enter being paid to look away.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Vanuatu at 3 out of 10, a low score, but scores its courts, police and watchdogs at only 4.9, in the middle of the range. Experts judge that officials here are not often working for criminal or outside interests, while the bodies meant to catch it if they were are only moderately able to do so.

For ni-Vanuatu, as the country's people are called, that single conviction shows the border can be opened for a fee by one person, and the middling strength of the courts and watchdogs means anything larger would take time to come to light.

Yemen.d:
Yemen's state has split in two since the war began in 2014, and outside governments have people in both halves. A Saudi government body, the 'Special Committee', kept about 2,700 Yemeni political, tribal and military leaders on monthly pay, according to records from 2012, and gave instructions to named sheikhs and a serving brigade commander. UN investigators report a similar arrangement by the United Arab Emirates, which they say pays several brigades inside the forces fighting the Houthis and commands the guard units at its own bases.

In the north the Houthi movement, a Zaydi Shia armed group, took the capital Sanaa and its institutions in 2014-15 and rules most of Yemen's population. UN investigators report foreign hands inside that administration too: a general of Iran's Quds Force, the foreign arm of its Revolutionary Guards, advising the Houthi leader and said to supervise the missile and naval forces; the man who buys weapons for the defence ministry in Sanaa attached to an office in Tehran; and an expert linked to Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed movement, alleged to guide the committee that sets customs duties, taxes and telephone tariffs and plans military spending. These are reports to a UN panel, not court findings. The Houthis have also put their own people in charge of the state airline and kept about $100 million of its cash.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Yemen's courts, police and watchdogs at 1.9 out of 10 and officials acting for criminal interests at 8. For Yemenis, the sheikhs and commanders who decide local matters may be paid by a foreign government, the duties and tariffs they pay in the north are set on advice from outside, and there is no court or police force to turn to when an armed group takes their land or money.

Algeria.d:
In Algeria the documented reach-in comes from two directions: foreign firms paying officials for state contracts, and the cocaine trade buying protection inside the security state.

Contractors have worked on the public works ministry, Sonatrach, the state oil and gas company, and the state telephone operator, usually through agents. The clearest example is the East-West motorway, begun in 2006 by Japanese and Chinese consortia: in 2015 an Algiers court jailed an adviser to the Chinese group, a former director of highways and other ministry staff over kickbacks on the project, whose cost rose from $6 billion to at least $13 billion. A court also convicted men from the Chinese telecoms suppliers ZTE and Huawei over about $10 million said to have reached an executive of Algérie Télécom whose contract decisions then favoured them, and the energy minister from 1999 to 2010 was sentenced in absentia to 20 years for corruption.

The cocaine trade reached into the police. When 701 kilograms of cocaine were found at the port of Oran in 2018, hidden in a cargo of imported meat, press reports tied the importer to judges, prosecutors, mayors and the children of senior politicians. The seizure brought down the head of the national police, and he and several generals were later convicted of corruption and illicit enrichment rather than drug offences; Algeria has published little about who protected the shipments.

Not every attempt succeeded. A British defence electronics group admitted in a 2026 UK agreement that its agents, on commissions of about 30 per cent, worked named officials of the Algiers airport authority and the post and technology ministry; both bids failed, and the court made no findings against any individual. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Algeria 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For Algerians, public money for roads, energy and phone networks has passed through officials who took a share, while the officials who let cocaine through a state port have not been named in court.

Argentina.d:
Argentina's state has more than once been run from inside by secret circles. Officers' lodges made and unmade the first governments after 1812 and, by most historians' account, organised the 1943 coup behind Juan Perón's rise. In the 1970s P2, a secret Masonic lodge run from Italy, listed an interim president, ministers, a junta member and generals among its members, and they gave its grand master a diplomatic post.

Since the 1990s the route has run more through business and money. A team of economists from a business-funded think tank took over the economy ministry in 1991, and its programme ended in frozen savings and the 2001 collapse. Firms have paid for state business under governments of left and right: a German engineering company admitted paying more than $100 million in bribes for a national identity-card contract, and in the notebooks case 87 people, including former president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, who denies it, are on trial over contractors' cash allegedly paid to officials. Other charges concern insurance commissions steered to a president's circle and, under the current government, kickbacks at the disability agency, which the accused deny.

Crime reaches police, courts and city halls. Around Rosario, drug and gambling bosses have had a provincial police chief, detectives who warned of raids and the city's chief prosecutor on their side. In Paraná a court found that a drug clan financed the winning mayor's campaign and was then given control of a municipal unit, which he denied. Federal judges, who hear drug cases, have been convicted of selling traffickers rulings or house arrest. For people in these places, the detective, prosecutor or judge may be on the gangs' side, and money for disabled people's medicines is alleged to have gone to people close to those spending it.

Azerbaijan.d:
Azerbaijan's economy rests on oil and gas, and the state oil company, SOCAR, is closely bound up with the government. Outsiders have got in by sharing state wealth with the officials who control it, or with people close to them. In the late 1990s investors trying to buy SOCAR in a privatisation they expected to be rigged made senior Azerbaijani officials their secret partners. A French rail engineering firm was found to have won its Baku metro contract corruptly, paying about 30 per cent of its invoices to an agent close to the minister in charge.

The state says foreign spy services have bought their way into its own security apparatus. Its State Security Service has announced that a foreign agency paid a reserve officer to win a post back inside the intelligence agencies, and that another recruited a serving department head in the national security ministry Both come from the security service itself, which names no foreign agency, and neither has been tested in a court that rules against the government.

Azerbaijani money reaches outward too. When Azerbaijan hosted the UN climate summit, COP29, in 2024, its president had been a SOCAR vice-president and its chief executive was filmed discussing oil and gas deals with campaigners posing as investors. An inquiry for the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly, Europe's human rights body, reported in 2018 a strong suspicion that some members acted for Azerbaijan in return for money or gifts, known as caviar diplomacy.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Azerbaijan 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4 for its courts and watchdogs. For people living there, oil wealth and public works budgets have been shared privately with foreign firms, and almost everything that can be checked came from abroad.

Barbados.d:
Barbados has one documented case of an outside party reaching into its government, and it came from a company seeking state business rather than from organised crime or a foreign state. Senior executives of the Insurance Corporation of Barbados Limited paid the island's Minister of Industry, Donville Inniss, about $36,000 in 2015 and 2016 to help the company win two government insurance contracts covering more than $100 million of state property. The money went through a US bank account in the name of a friend's dental company in New York, which is why a US jury, not a Barbadian court, convicted him of money laundering in 2020; he was sentenced to two years in prison.

No other case of a foreign government, company, crime group or lodge placing people or money inside the state remains on this map. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Barbados 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 6.1 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, better than most of the Caribbean. Barbados is also an offshore financial centre that registers international companies, the kind of business that can draw outside money.

For Barbadians, this means a minister used his office to steer the insurance of public property to a company that paid him, and the case came to light only because the money passed through the United States. The likeliest places for outside money to reach in are the ones this case shows: who wins public contracts, who funds politicians and who owns the companies registered on the island.

Benin.d:
Benin has one documented case, and it reaches the unit closest to the president. In 2024 a court convicted the businessman Olivier Boko over money handed to the officer commanding the presidential guard; prosecutors said the payment was meant to turn that unit against the president it protects. The money came from private wealth rather than a foreign state, and what it bought was an officer with troops rather than a policy or a contract.

Beyond that, little is documented. Benin is a coastal West African state whose port at Cotonou handles goods for its larger neighbour, Nigeria, and for landlocked states to the north, so much of the trade crossing it belongs to outsiders. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Benin 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3.8 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That combination describes officials under real pressure with weak checks on them.

For people living there, the proven case shows private money reaching inside the armed unit that guards the head of state, which is also the kind of case a government has a strong reason to bring. Whether outside interests are paying officials in port and customs work, public contracts or policing is not documented, so there is no named company or official residents can challenge over it.

Botswana.d:
Botswana's first documented case reaches the minister in charge of its mines and its power supply. Prosecutors charged in 2025 that payments from Sieyuan Electric and New Energy Company, firms seeking licences and power contracts, reached the Minister of Mineral Resources, Green Technology and Energy Security, and that he then signed eight licences for one of them. These are charges, not a conviction, and nothing has yet been proven against him.

Licences are where the value sits in this economy. Botswana's wealth rests on diamonds, mined mainly through a long-standing partnership between the government and the De Beers company, and the minister who signs a licence decides who may dig, and who may sell power into the grid. That is the office the charges describe being paid.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Botswana 4.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.4 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That puts it in the middle of the range and ahead of most of its neighbours, and it is a Botswana court, not a foreign one, hearing this case. For people living there, that is where they can see what the evidence shows about who was paying for the licences issued over their minerals.

Burkina Faso.d:
No documented case in Burkina Faso yet meets the map's test, which asks for an outside party that got its people, money or control inside a government body or company and had decisions there serve it. This entry is an estimate.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Burkina Faso high for officials working for criminal interests, and very weak in the courts, police and watchdogs that would check them. On those scores, a criminal group or foreign interest trying to place people inside the state, or to buy officials already there, would meet little resistance at home, and the record of it would be thin. The country has been under military government since 2022, and nothing here reaches into that government.

Cameroon.d:
Two cases in Cameroon meet the map's test, and both were proved in courts abroad. The commodity trader Glencore paid bribes to officials of Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures and Société Nationale de Raffinage, Cameroon's state oil and refining companies, for favourable treatment in the allocation and sale of crude and the purchase of oil products. An English court put the Cameroon bribes at EUR 10,532,712 between March 2012 and March 2015: EUR 4,187,820 disguised as service fees under an agent's contract, and EUR 6,344,892 in cash drawn from Glencore's Swiss cash desk. Glencore's UK arm pleaded guilty in London in June 2022 to seven counts, five of them bribery, and was fined GBP 182,935,392 in all, of which GBP 56,881,245 was for the Cameroon count. The judge said he made no findings against any individual, and individuals remained under Serious Fraud Office investigation, uncharged.

The second runs through arms buying. Defex S.A., the arms export company majority-owned by the Spanish state, supplied Cameroon's government with maritime surveillance patrol boats, parts and training between 2005 and 2013. Spain's Audiencia Nacional found in February 2023 that Defex's commercial director and the head of a subcontractor paid trips, hotel stays and cosmetic surgery for the wife of a senior Cameroonian official, to win goodwill and to obtain and keep the contracts; both men got two years, upheld by Spain's Supreme Court in September 2026. That judgment names no individual Cameroonian official.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cameroon among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as weak. Paul Biya has held the presidency since 1982, so an inquiry starting inside the country would have to start inside a government that has not changed hands in that time. Both cases fit that picture: the money moved through Cameroon's state oil companies and its defence purchasing, and in each it was a foreign prosecutor and a foreign court that established it.

Chile.d:
In Chile, outsiders have reached the state through three routes: foreign intelligence money during the Cold War, companies paying the officials who write laws, collect taxes and decide cases, and crime groups buying the officers who police them.

Between 1963 and 1973 the CIA spent about $13 million on Chilean parties, candidates and a newspaper, and under Pinochet it kept the head of the secret police as a paid contact.

Since the return to democracy the money has come mostly from companies, reaching each branch of the state. A holding group used employees inside the tax service to pass campaign money through fake invoices. A fishing company paid a senator, later jailed for bribery, who voted its way on the 2012 fisheries law that handed a large share of the national catch to a few families' companies. In 2026 a Supreme Court justice was detained, accused of taking money from a mining-truck consortium over a ruling in which her chamber ordered Codelco, the state copper company, to pay the consortium $20 million rather than the reverse. Bodies outside the state go the same way: marketing companies' payments bought the head of Chile's football association, who pleaded guilty in the US. The armed forces have been reached by sellers too: a judge ruled in 2017 that a broker had delivered about 15 million dollars in commissions to senior air force officers over the 1994 purchase of 25 Mirage aircraft, and a retired general was convicted of taking 65,000 dollars of it.

As Chile has become a drug transit route, the buying has reached the police and prisons. National police officers have been charged with reselling seized drugs and protecting dealers, detectives of the investigative police convicted of selling a ketamine gang the warrants and evidence against it, and in 2025 about a tenth of the guards at Santiago's main remand prison charged with smuggling drugs and phones to gangs held there. For Chileans, laws, tax checks and court rulings can be bought by the firms they concern, and in some places the officers policing a gang are working for it.

Congo, Dem. Rep..d:
Congo has been reached from outside in two ways: by neighbouring armies and the armed groups they back, and by foreign companies paying for its mines, forests and state contracts. In the 1960s the CIA paid Joseph Mobutu, who went on to rule until 1997. After a Rwandan-backed rebellion ended his rule, a Rwandan officer served as chief of staff of Congo's army.

The live case is M23, a rebel force that took the eastern cities of Goma and Bukavu in 2025. UN sanctions monitors report that Rwanda's army commands it and that Rwandans have been put in charge of mining, tax, banking and border control; Rwanda denies it. Kinshasa says the reach goes into its own state: military courts have sentenced to death a sitting MP who owned a coltan mine and, in his absence, Joseph Kabila, president until 2019, and a former eastern commander is on trial for treason. All three deny it, and reports from that trial say the prosecution has struggled to prove contact with Rwanda.

Companies reach in through intermediaries, and buy the officials meant to check them. US authorities say a commodity trader and a New York hedge fund sent money through third parties to reach Congolese officials and win mining business; both settled. Chinese logging companies are reported to have paid the officials who allocate forest concessions and oversee what is cut, obtaining concessions during a moratorium and cover for felling above quota.

For people in the east, the governors and tax collectors over them have been appointed by a group that UN monitors say a foreign army commands. Across Congo, money from mines, timber and state contracts has gone to insiders, and the Global Organized Crime Index rates the country among the worst in the world for officials working for criminal interests.

Croatia.d:
Croatia's documented cases show companies and wealthy men reaching the state through the people who decide: ministers at the top of government, and judges. The clearest is the national oil company, INA. MOL, a Hungarian oil company in which the Hungarian state has influence, wanted to run it, and Croatian courts found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL's chief executive to give it that control. MOL denies the bribe, and Hungary has not handed the executive over to Croatia.

The pattern continues in health and in the courts. In 2024 the health minister was arrested and sacked, accused of taking bribes from a group selling medical equipment to approve hospital purchases at inflated prices; prosecutors say tenders were fixed at least four times, two hospital directors are among those charged, and the minister denies it. Prosecutors have also charged a football executive facing trial with paying three judges of the county court hearing his cases, so that its rulings would suit him; he denies it.

For Croatians, the national oil company they part-own is still managed by the firm the courts found paid their prime minister for that control, hospitals may have paid more for equipment because the minister in charge was paid by the sellers, and a defendant with money may have been judged by people on his payroll. Croatian courts can punish the officials who take the money but not always those who pay it: the MOL executive lives in another EU country that will not send him back. The courts have reached a former head of government, though it took most of a decade.

Denmark.d:
Very little outside reach into the Danish state or Danish companies is documented on the map, and what there is comes from two directions: a foreign spy service working through an insider, and a business-led network at the head of state.

Russian intelligence has paid people working inside Denmark to collect information. In the clearest case, a Russian man employed by a Danish fuel cell maker spent several years gathering information on energy technology from that company and from the Technical University of Denmark and passing it to Russian intelligence for money; a court in Aalborg sentenced him in 2021 to three years in prison and permanent expulsion. Russia called the case a witch hunt.

King Frederik X is listed among alumni of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, which he joined as crown prince. The Forum is the Swiss-based organisation behind the annual Davos meeting of business and political leaders, and its programme gathers people under about 40 into a five-year network of meetings and courses. The king's role is ceremonial, so the membership does not show the Forum deciding anything for Danes, only that its network reaches the office that formally heads the state.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Denmark among the very lowest countries in the world for officials working for criminal interests, and among the strongest for its courts, police and watchdogs. For Danes, this means the officials they deal with are unlikely to be working for criminal or foreign interests, and the documented risk sits with the research and energy firms that foreign intelligence wants to learn from.

Ecuador.d:
Ecuador sits between the two largest cocaine-producing countries, Colombia and Peru, and its Pacific ports have become one of the main exits for cocaine bound for Europe and the United States. The gangs that run this trade pay the officials at each point the drugs, the money and their own members pass through. At the coast they recruit port workers and customs officers so that cocaine hidden in banana shipments leaving Guayaquil passes inspection. Inland they buy judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison staff, so that members are released, cases are delayed and the gangs learn what investigators know. Decrypted messages on one trafficker's phone led to the conviction of 20 people, among them the former head of the council that oversees Ecuador's judges.

Foreign companies and businessmen reach in through the money. Oil traders, contractors and builders from abroad have paid officials at Petroecuador, the state oil company, and in the ministries above it, reaching two vice-presidents. The bodies meant to catch this have been bought too: Odebrecht, the Brazilian builder, paid Ecuador's Comptroller General, whose office audits state spending, more than $10 million to cancel the fines on its projects, and British brokers paid the chairman of two state insurers to steer their reinsurance business to them.

For people in Ecuador a court ruling or a release may have been bought, the soldiers, port staff and police around them may be on a gang's payroll, and the auditor who should have fined a contractor was taking its money instead, while the bribes came out of the oil revenue and loans that pay for schools, hospitals and power. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials working for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10, with the courts and watchdogs meant to resist them at under 4.5.

Eritrea.d:
This is an estimate: no case on the map names a foreign government, company or criminal group placing or paying people inside Eritrea's government. Eritrea has been governed by one party, the People's Front for Democracy and Justice, since independence in 1993, has held no national election in that time and has no independent press, so very little can be checked from outside.

What reporting there is points to criminal business run from inside the state rather than reaching in from outside. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 9.5 out of 10, one of the highest scores in the world, and says military officers and ruling-party members dominate smuggling of people, gold, alcohol, tobacco and counterfeit goods, much of it across the border with Sudan, and that officials involved are rarely prosecuted. A 2013 report presented at the European Parliament said the army's border surveillance unit took part in smuggling Eritreans into Sudan, where thousands are reported to have died in captivity.

If that picture is right, Eritreans who try to leave the country pay the same officers who are meant to guard the border, and money from gold and trade ends up in private hands. The strength of courts and watchdogs scores 2.2 out of 10, and there is no independent body inside the country where a resident could take a complaint.

Fiji.d:
Fiji sits on the shipping and air routes that carry methamphetamine and cocaine across the Pacific to Australia and New Zealand, and traffickers moving those drugs have got inside its police and customs. The minister for policing told parliament in 2025 that 27 police officers had been involved in 33 drug cases since the start of 2023. Two officers of the counter-narcotics unit and a senior customs manager were among seven people charged with helping methamphetamine through Nadi airport in air cargo, and the unit was later disbanded. Leaked chats published in late 2025 appeared to show senior officers discussing drug shipments and payments with traffickers; the police commissioner confirmed that seven senior officers were under investigation, and the claims have not been tested in court.

Business money has also tried to reach officials. Two men from a Chinese company in Fiji pleaded guilty in 2010 to offering the top civil servant in the finance ministry money and tea for help with a water project; both received prison terms. The anti-corruption commission has more recently charged a businessman with earlier drug and trafficking convictions with bribing officials of the iTaukei Land Trust Board, which manages land owned by Fiji's indigenous people; the outcome of that trial could not be confirmed.

For people in Fiji, the officers responsible for stopping drugs at the airport and the border may be working for those bringing them in, and indigenous landowners face an allegation that the body handling their land was paid by a businessman. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 4 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.4, a middle position in which cases are being investigated and charged rather than ignored.

Gambia.d:
Under Yahya Jammeh, president from 1994 to 2017, The Gambia's state businesses were handed to a small circle around him, and part of that circle was tied to a foreign armed movement. Lebanese businessmen whom the United States designates as financiers of Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shia party and armed group, received state monopolies, including the national fuel supply and half of the state telephone companies. OCCRP, a network of investigative reporters, estimated that more than $100 million from Gambian telecoms reached Hezbollah.

For Gambians, this meant they paid for fuel and telephone calls through monopolies given to the president's associates, and some of that money left the country to fund a foreign armed group rather than reaching the treasury. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.

Greece.d:
Greece's record shows two lasting ways in: organised groups getting inside the armed forces, police and ports, and bankers buying their way into the state's finances. A secret society of army officers, IDEA, grew inside the army and its members led the 1967 coup. The neo-Nazi party Golden Dawn later built support inside the police: after the May 2012 election, polling stations used by Attica police officers gave it just over 20 per cent of the vote against about 6 per cent at civilian stations nearby, and its leaders were convicted in 2020 of running a criminal organisation.

The reach goes on today, following whatever is being moved. Foreign intelligence services recruit serving officers, among them an air force colonel charged in 2026 with passing NATO plans to Chinese handlers. Criminal groups recruit the people who control access: prosecutors say an Athens ring selling 'protection' to nightlife venues had at least 11 police officers as members; cocaine networks use dockers at Piraeus, the largest port, to empty containers; and five officers of a border guard unit on the Evros frontier are charged with arranging crossings for the smuggling ring paying them.

Money has been the other way in: a bank owner said he had paid the prime minister and ministers, who in return had state companies deposit public money in his bank; two were convicted in 1992.

Foreign companies have bought decisions at the top of the state. Greece ordered three German Type 214 submarines in 2000 for 1.26 billion euros and a fourth in 2002; a German court fined Ferrostaal 40 million euros in 2011 and convicted two of its managers over the bribes paid to win the order, Bremen prosecutors found the sensor supplier Atlas Elektronik had paid as much as 13 million euros in commissions, and in 2013 defence minister Akis Tsochatzopoulos was jailed for 20 years for laundering about 75 million dollars tied to the submarines and a Russian missile buy, the bribery charges themselves having run out of time. The deputy head of defence procurement admitted taking money and testified against the rest. Bremen prosecutors fined Rheinmetall 37 million euros over an air-defence deal, finding that commissions to a Greek agent had partly funded bribes to Greek officials, and a Greek court in 2018 sentenced 17 people over the money paid around Ericsson's sale of airborne radar systems. Siemens worked the same way on the civil side: an Athens court convicted transport minister Tassos Mantelis in 2017 of laundering 450,000 deutsche marks from the company, paid around his approval of a contract between its Greek unit and the state telecoms firm OTE, and a parliamentary report put the cost to the state at at least 2 billion euros.

For people in Greece, this means migrants and opponents policed by officers many of whom backed a criminal organisation, nightlife businesses paying a ring that included the police meant to protect them, and the men guarding the border and the port's cargo accused of working for the traffickers crossing them. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5.1.

Guinea-Bissau.d:
Since the mid-2000s Guinea-Bissau, a small West African country with weak central control, has been a transit point for South American cocaine headed to Europe. The trafficking networks reached the commanders of the armed forces themselves. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research group, reports that Latin American trafficking cells were paying the military for protection by about 2006, that this protection went right to the top, and that senior military figures took control of bulk transit and kept a share of the profits, reportedly 13% to 15%. Those are the group's findings from its sources, with no court verdict behind them.

In 2013 US prosecutors charged the heads of the navy, the air force and the army with offering their positions to help move cocaine. The army chief, who had led a coup the year before, was also charged with offering to store cocaine for the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army, and sell it weapons. Only the navy chief was caught, in a sting at sea; the other two stayed in Bissau and were never handed over.

The armed forces have repeatedly overthrown or threatened elected governments, so the people accused of taking traffickers' money are the same people who decide who governs. The reach also extends to the justice system: traffickers convicted over the country's largest cocaine seizure reportedly got out of prison on fake sick notes.

For people in Guinea-Bissau, this means the officers commanding their army, navy and air force have been accused of working for foreign traffickers, and those accused have remained free and in some cases in power. With the courts and watchdogs scoring under 2.7 out of 10 on the Global Organized Crime Index and officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5, the cases against them have been brought abroad.

Hungary.d:
Hungary's documented cases show foreign intelligence services working through Hungarians who hold European posts. Russia's services had a Hungarian member of the European Parliament working for them: Béla Kovács, elected for the nationalist party Jobbik, was convicted in Hungary in 2022 of spying on EU institutions for Russia and lives in Russia. Hungary's own intelligence service has used its position in Brussels in a similar way, with officers under diplomatic cover at Hungary's mission to the EU trying for years to recruit Hungarians employed at the European Commission, the EU's executive, a network the Commission has confirmed.

Both run through the same opening: Hungarians who hold seats or jobs in EU institutions have access to information and decisions that affect all 27 member states, which makes them worth recruiting for Moscow and for Budapest's own government. Hungary has also been on the receiving end of a foreign power placing its own people in charge. In October 1944 Nazi Germany detained the regent and installed the leader of the Arrow Cross, Hungary's fascist movement, as head of government; in under three months its death squads killed up to 38,000 Hungarian Jews.

Inside Hungary today, the Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 7.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 4.8, a weak position for an EU member. For people in Hungary, this means a representative they elected to the European Parliament was working for a foreign intelligence service, and Hungarians working in EU institutions have been targeted by their own country's spies, so decisions that affect their rights, funds and trade are taken with a foreign or partisan service listening in.

Iran.d:
In Iran the documented reach into the state has come above all from foreign intelligence services, along with foreign oil money. In 1953 the CIA, with British help, bribed members of parliament and organised the security forces to remove the elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, after he nationalised Iran's oil; the Shah then ruled as a US ally until the 1979 revolution.

Since the revolution, the agency Iran most often accuses of recruiting people inside its state is Israel's foreign intelligence service, Mossad. Iranian officials said in 2024 that Mossad had hired guards from the Revolutionary Guards unit that protects senior officials to plant the bombs that killed the Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh in a Guards guesthouse in Tehran; Israel neither confirmed nor denied it. Iran has also hanged a nuclear institute scientist as a Mossad agent, without making the evidence public, and a former deputy defence minister as a British spy, a charge he said was extracted under torture.

The oil sector has also been reached with money. A Paris court convicted a French oil company in 2018 of corrupting foreign officials through about $30 million in disguised consulting payments connected to a deal on the South Pars gas field; prosecutors said much of it was meant for a former president's son, who then ran subsidiaries of the national oil company.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Iran 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 3 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Iran this means no independent court or free press can examine which foreign services or companies have people inside the state, and anyone accused of spying is tried, and may be executed, by courts that are not independent of the government bringing the charge.

Italy.d:
Italy's mafias get inside the state mostly at the level of the town hall and the local health service. The exchange is votes: a clan delivers them at election time and then has a say over public jobs, building contracts, permits and hospital services. Since 1991 the national government has dissolved town councils and local health authorities 402 times after finding them under mafia control, mostly in the south but also in the north and around Rome. It continues: four more councils were dissolved in 2025 after mayors near Rome, outside Naples and in Sicily were arrested or sentenced over alleged vote deals with clans, one of them Caserta, a provincial capital.

Companies and secret networks have reached further up. In the early 1990s the 'Mani pulite' inquiry found that firms paid the governing parties a cut of public works contracts, and at one point more than half of parliament was under indictment. A decade earlier police seized the membership list of P2, a hidden Masonic lodge, with 962 names on it: members of parliament, serving ministers, nearly 200 senior military officers and the heads of all three intelligence services.

Individual officials are bought too. Prosecutors say a private data firm had serving police and tax-police officers on its payroll searching state databases for its paying clients, and Russian military intelligence has paid a navy officer on the defence staff for classified documents.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Italy 7 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and above 6 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in southern Italy especially, an elected council can be replaced by commissioners for up to two years, and public works and hospital services can go to firms a clan controls.

Kazakhstan.d:
Kazakhstan's state draws most of its money from oil and gas, and most of the documented cases of outsiders reaching in run the same way: Western companies competing for the country's fields and pipelines paid consultants and agents, knowing the money would reach the Kazakh officials who decided who got the work. The pattern is not confined to energy. France's financial prosecutor found that a European aerospace group, competing for the national space agency's satellite work, engaged an intermediary mainly to introduce it to a businessman close to the president so that he would intercede with the authorities, then routed the promised commission through companies in Ireland, the Isle of Man and Hong Kong to get around its own compliance checks. US and British settlements record a US oilfield services company and a British engineering group paying, or intending to pay, officials of the state oil company and of a pipeline venture owned by the Kazakh and Chinese governments.

US prosecutors charged in 2003 that an American adviser to President Nursultan Nazarbayev had moved about $20 million through Swiss accounts to the president and a former prime minister for Western firms' oil contracts. The adviser pleaded guilty only to a tax offence in 2010, so the bribery claims against Kazakh leaders were never proven in court. Kazakhstan itself now claims, in a confidential London arbitration, that foreign contractors bribed its officials to approve costs at the Karachaganak gas field; leaks say the panel accepted some of this, but no ruling has been published.

Evidence of a foreign state getting someone inside is thinner. In 2019 a China expert at a state-run institute, reported to advise on border talks, was jailed for treason. Media reports said he passed documents to China, but details were never published, he pleaded not guilty, and he was later pardoned.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kazakhstan 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 5 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people in Kazakhstan, this means the contracts for the oil and gas that fund their state have repeatedly been won by paying officials, and most of what is known comes from foreign prosecutors and leaks.

Korea, Rep..d:
In South Korea, three kinds of outside force have reached into politics and the state: religious movements, through gifts, cash and mass sign-ups to a party; business, through payments and deals with officials; and the spy services of North Korea and China, through recruits in parties and the armed forces. In 2026 the leader of the Unification Church, a Korean-founded movement, was sentenced for arranging luxury gifts for the first lady and cash for a senior lawmaker of the then-governing People Power Party; the church will appeal. Investigators say thousands of its followers and at least 56,000 from another movement, Shincheonji, joined that party. A minister from the rival Democratic Party resigned over similar cash claims, which he denies.

Samsung, the largest family-run business group, has been found by courts to have bribed two presidents' circles, and those convicted were later pardoned. Developers worked with a planning chief at a city-owned company to fix a housing project's terms, costing it about 490 billion won, a court found.

North Korea's ruling party has run cells that placed members in the leadership of a party with seats in the National Assembly. Both neighbours recruit in the military with cash, and the record reaches the bodies meant to catch them: an employee of military intelligence sold a Chinese agent the identities of undercover officers abroad, while two heads of its secret operations team and a counter-espionage officer have been accused of leaking secrets, with no reported verdict.

Foreign suppliers have reached state research as well: a British maker of seismic equipment admitted in a UK agreement that it paid more than $1m over twelve years to a senior figure at the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources, who shaped specifications to fit its products, advised it on pricing and passed it a rival's bid. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials working for outside interests at 4 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 8. For South Koreans this means churches have sought influence through a first lady and a party's membership, and companies have bought favours from presidents and city officials, though courts have convicted many involved.

Laos.d:
Laos has one documented case, and it is at the border. In 2023 the government disciplined 78 police and immigration officers at the Boten checkpoint for letting Chinese nationals through without recording them. The officers had been paid by people who wanted to cross unchecked, so the country's immigration control stopped working at the point where it is actually applied, and there is no record of who entered or left while it did.

That is the only case on the record here, and the record is thin for a reason. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Laos 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs: officials can work for criminal groups with little risk of being exposed, and the one case that did come to light was handled as internal discipline rather than in court, so no evidence about who was paying was ever tested in public.

For people in Laos this means the border post that is supposed to record who comes into the country was run, for a time, for whoever paid the officers on duty, and there is no independent body whose findings would show whether the officials who govern them answer to someone else.

Liberia.d:
In Liberia, outside bodies have shaped how state money is spent, and traffickers have reached into the police and the prosecution. After the civil wars, international lenders reached directly into the state firms. Under a 2005 programme designed and funded by the IMF, the World Bank and the US government, foreign financial controllers sat inside the port authority, the main airport, the state oil refiner and the forestry agency with power to co-sign their major transactions, until signing authority returned to Liberian hands in 2009.

Today the documented pressure comes from cocaine traffickers using Liberia as a stop on the route from South America to Europe, and it runs through the offices that decide whether a case proceeds. The US Treasury sanctioned Liberia's Solicitor General and chief prosecutor in 2022, saying people facing prosecution and money launderers paid him to drop their cases. After the country's largest recorded seizure in 2026, nearly four tonnes bound for Europe, police charged the head of their own major crimes unit, named a senior airport security officer as a participant, and said senior government officials were involved; these are charges and a designation, not convictions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Liberia 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for its courts and watchdogs. For Liberians this means that the police unit meant to fight serious crime, the officer guarding the main airport and the lawyer who decides who gets prosecuted have each been accused of working for the other side, so a drug case can be stopped at the airport, at the police station or in the prosecutor's office.

Luxembourg.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Luxembourg, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people inside its government.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, rates Luxembourg among the lowest in the world on that measure. That means experts judge that officials there rarely act for criminal interests.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party, and the index suggests officials face less of this pressure than in most countries. If outside money did reach in, it would most likely show up in who funds politicians, who wins public contracts and who sits on the boards of companies the state regulates, and residents are best protected when those records are public.

Maldives.d:
The Maldives sits between India and China's shipping routes in the Indian Ocean, and the one recorded claim of an outside power reaching inside its politics comes from that rivalry. In December 2024 the Washington Post reported that Maldivian opposition politicians had planned to pay 40 members of parliament, including some from President Mohamed Muizzu's own party, to vote to impeach him, using about $6 million to be sought from India. Muizzu had won office promising to reduce India's influence. The paper said an officer of India's foreign intelligence agency explored ways to remove him through two intermediaries, who confirmed the plan existed. No money is reported to have been paid, Muizzu's coalition won a parliamentary majority in 2024, and a former president denied any Indian role.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates the Maldives in the middle range for how far officials work for criminal or outside interests, and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as fairly weak. Conditions like that usually mean some officials can be paid to serve business or criminal interests and the bodies meant to catch them have gaps.

For Maldivians, this means the members of parliament they elect have been treated, at least in planning, as votes a foreign-backed group could buy to remove their president. In daily life the weak institutions are more likely to show as bribes asked for ordinary services and state contracts going to favoured firms.

Mauritania.d:
No case has yet been documented of a foreign state, company or crime group paying Mauritanian officials or placing people inside the government, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions.

Mauritania lies on the route by which South American cocaine crosses the Sahara and the Sahel towards North Africa and Europe. The UN Office on Drugs and Crime reported in 2024 that across Mauritania and its Sahel neighbours, traffickers include members of the political elite and use their profits to get into state institutions and avoid prosecution, and Mauritania itself has made some of the largest cocaine seizures in the region. The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials there often serving criminal interests and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as weak.

If the estimate is right, the pressure would show most in policing and border control, and people in Mauritania would face traffickers who are protected by officials rather than stopped by them. Without a named case there is no official or company they can yet hold to account.

Moldova.d:
Moldova's courts, banks and elected offices have been used by outside money, most of it Russian, on a scale few countries match. In the scheme known as the Global Laundromat, Russian companies signed fake debts that Moldovan judges ordered paid into a Moldovan bank, moving tens of billions of dollars out of Russia; prosecutors later charged judges who approved them. In 2014 about $1 billion, roughly 12 percent of the country's economic output, vanished from three banks including the state savings bank, and a former prime minister was jailed for taking money to let a businessman's investors take control of it.

Russian money has also paid for political parties and candidates, and the accusations reach as high as the presidency. Igor Dodon, president from 2016 to 2020 and leader of the pro-Russian Socialist Party, was filmed saying his party received monthly funding from Russia and has been charged with high treason and illegal party financing; his trial is being restarted. Courts have banned a party for serving a foreign state's interests and sentenced a regional governor and a member of parliament for channelling undeclared money to that network in elections. The MP, who denies it, was sentenced in his absence. Prosecutors also say an assistant to Russia's military attaché ran the head of parliament's legal division and a senior border police officer at Chișinău airport; both are on trial for treason.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Moldova widely serving criminal interests. For Moldovans this means a court ruling could be bought by a foreign client, the savings they and the state held in the banks were taken with help from people running the government, and some of those they elected owed their campaigns to foreign money. If the charges against Dodon hold, that includes a president.

Morocco.d:
Morocco is one of the world's main producers of cannabis resin and lies on routes that carry cocaine across the Sahara and North Africa to Europe. Traffickers on these routes need officials and elected figures who can protect property, permits and shipments, and the record shows one network reaching them. A drug-trafficking network linked to a Malian trafficker known as the 'Escobar of the Sahara' drew Moroccan elected figures and security staff into its operation: in 2026 a Casablanca court jailed a former president of the Oriental regional council, a former member of parliament and the former president of the Wydad Casablanca football club, and gave shorter terms to local officials, security officers and gendarmes, a military police force, for helping drug lorries pass through. The case is under appeal.

The other documented case involves a foreign company. US regulators found that the German dialysis firm Fresenius bribed the chief kidney specialist at two state-owned military hospitals for about four years to win contracts there, and it paid a settlement covering Morocco and other countries in 2019.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Morocco often serving criminal interests. For Moroccans this means that, in the trafficking case, the court found the head of a regional council and gendarmes at the roadside working for traffickers rather than for the people who elected or employ them, and in the hospital case contracts were won by paying the hospitals' senior kidney doctor. These are the only two documented cases on the map for Morocco, so how far either pattern reaches beyond them is not shown by the record.

Nauru.d:
In Nauru, a small Pacific island state whose main export is phosphate, outside money arrives mainly from Australia, and it has reached the island's politicians through the two things Australia buys there: phosphate and the hosting of asylum seekers.

Australian businesspeople seeking phosphate deals have been prosecuted in Australia for paying Nauruan politicians; one Sydney businessman was jailed in 2018 for paying an MP and a minister, and a Gold Coast phosphate trader is still awaiting trial on a charge of conspiring to bribe them. The second channel is the asylum detention centre that Australia pays contractors to run on the island. In 2023 the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age reported that subcontracts worth millions went to firms tied to Nauru's leaders, with banking records showing suspect payments to the justice minister and to a company of a man who later became president. The reporters said they were not claiming the payments were bribes, the minister denies wrongdoing, and Australia's Home Affairs department had been warned of bribery allegations for more than a decade.

In a country this small, a few contracts from one foreign government make up a large share of the money in circulation, and the politicians who decide on them can also benefit from them.

For people in Nauru this means that phosphate, one of the few sources of national income, has been sold through deals prosecutors say were bought, cutting what reaches the public. Ministers who benefit from Australian contracts have a private reason to keep the detention centre open whatever residents want.

Nicaragua.d:
In Nicaragua the reach into the state has come from two very different directions: the United States in the past, and drug traffickers more recently. In 1911 and 1912 New York bankers, backed by Washington, lent Nicaragua money against its National Bank as collateral and a majority stake in the National Railway, while the US president appointed its customs collector; when the president they dealt with faced a revolt, US Marines landed and stayed until 1935. In the 1980s a foundation funded by the US Congress paid for opposition groups and the newspaper La Prensa before the 1990 election.

The recent cases point to traffickers reaching the bodies that issue identities and pass sentences. In 2012 a court convicted a magistrate of the Supreme Electoral Council, which oversees elections, of giving members of a trafficking network false identity cards, and he got 17 years. Two years earlier the interior minister said she held a list of judges who had granted releases or shorter sentences to 1,000 traffickers, though the report names no judge and no payment has been proven. Leaked US cables alleging that the ruling Sandinista party took traffickers' money have no reply on record.

Company money reached office-holders in other bodies: the man who ran the national football federation and then held a FIFA post pleaded guilty to taking money from the firms buying rights to the game.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Nicaragua one of the lowest scores in the world for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, and one of the highest for officials working for criminal or outside interests. For people in Nicaragua an official of the body that runs their elections has been shown to work for traffickers, and if others are, there is little domestic power to examine it.

Norway.d:
Norway is one of the countries where outside forces have the least documented hold on government. The Global Organized Crime Index gives it one of the world's lowest scores for officials working for criminal interests.

The exceptions the record shows are foreign spy services recruiting people with access, and a drug importer working with the police. The spy cases run from the Cold War to today. The KGB had an agent in Arne Treholt, a Labour Party official who sat in fishing and Law of the Sea talks with the Soviet Union and became head of the Foreign Ministry's press department before his arrest in 1984 and conviction for treason. The same approach is still used on people with less senior posts but useful access: in 2025 an Oslo court convicted a Norwegian security guard at the US embassy who had sold Russian and Iranian intelligence the embassy's floor plans, security routines and the home addresses of diplomats and their families.

Inside the police, drug enforcement depends on officers handling informants with little outside oversight. Eirik Jensen ran the Oslo police narcotics section for years while helping an informant he managed bring around fourteen tonnes of hashish into the country, and was jailed for twenty-one years, the most senior police conviction of its kind in Scandinavia.

For Norwegians, this has meant that a man passing information to the KGB took part in their country's sea-boundary talks with the Soviet Union, that the unit meant to stop the drug trade in Oslo was protecting one of its suppliers, and that foreign services can still find a guard or clerk willing to sell what he sees at work. In each case the courts held the person to account.

Panama.d:
Panama's place in the record comes from its role as a corridor for ships, money and companies, and from the people who have paid their way into its government and its ports because of it. Its law firms set up companies for clients abroad, its free zone in Colón lets goods pass without entering customs, and its banks have held money for traffickers and rulers alike.

Under military rule in the 1980s the state was rented out from the top. Manuel Noriega, the army commander who ran the country, took money from Colombia's Medellín cartel to make Panama a shipping platform for cocaine while also being paid as a CIA source. The largest recent reach came from Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group that admitted paying bribes across Latin America and Africa to win public contracts; it says it paid Panamanian officials during the 2009–2014 government, and the trial of more than 20 people, including a former president, opened in 2026.

Lower down, trafficking groups recruit the people who check the roads, the ships and the planes, and the record now reaches the president's own guard. A gang federation has paid police officers, including one who opened checkpoints and escorted its drug shipments; 26 workers at the Port of Balboa were arrested over cocaine hidden in export containers; and a cocaine ring working through the main airport has been convicted with officials of the presidential guard, the prosecution service, the air and naval service and airport security inside it.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Panama high for officials working for criminal interests. For residents, public contracts and protection from the law have been on offer to the corridor's biggest users, and the docks, the airport and the guard around the president have all had staff on a trafficking network's side.

Philippines.d:
In the Philippines the groups that reach into government are the ones that can deliver cash: illegal gambling operators, the contractors who live off public works, and foreign firms and spy services after contracts or secrets.

Gambling money has bought protection and sometimes the police themselves. Operators of jueteng, an illegal numbers game, were accused of paying President Joseph Estrada 5 million pesos a month. From 2016 Chinese-run online gambling hubs were helped by brokers who paid immigration officers to wave Chinese workers through Manila's airport, and by allies placed in local office, including a mayor a court later found to be a Chinese citizen. Congress banned the industry in 2025. In December 2025 prosecutors charged a businessman tied to cockfighting arenas and 14 serving police officers over the abduction of cockfight workers.

Public works and procurement are the largest channel now. In 2025 flood-control contractors told the Senate that lawmakers and public-works officials demanded 10 to 25 percent of each project as 'advance commissions'; the Speaker stepped down. US prosecutors charge that executives of a voting-technology firm bribed the head of the elections commission for the 2016 vote-counting contract, which they deny, and a Canadian supplier settled claims that it paid officials over twelve years to win the police contract for identifying bullets. Chinese intelligence pays civilian staff in the defence department, navy and coast guard; investigators say handlers posing as research clients got the navy's resupply plans that way.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores the Philippines high for officials working for criminal interests. For Filipinos this has meant flood defences skimmed by the people who approve them, towns run by officials loyal to a gambling compound, police gear and election machines bought, prosecutors allege, with bribes, and the navy's plans sold by the staff who held them.

Romania.d:
In Romania the documented reach-in is concentrated where goods and money cross the state's own checkpoints. Smuggling networks have not bought the odd customs officer but whole border posts: prosecutors indicted 41 officers at the Moravița crossing in 2011 over a cigarette route, and 66 at the Siret crossing the same year, in both places most of the staff there. Where that happens, the lorry search the state pays for becomes a service for the people it is meant to catch.

Public contracts are the other channel. In 2025 prosecutors detained a former transport minister, accusing him of acting for a company that wanted a state contract renewed and offering the director of the state's own automobile registry a cut of it. The case has not been tried.

The oldest case on the record is from 1940, when the fascist Iron Guard was given the Interior Ministry, the Bucharest police and all 50 county prefectures, the offices that run each county for the central government, and its men used that state power to kill opponents and Jews until the movement was expelled after a failed coup.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Romania in the middle range both for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For Romanians this means the border posts their taxes fund have worked for smugglers, a contract awarded in their name may have been arranged by a former minister for a fee, and the cases mostly stop at indictment rather than a verdict.

San Marino.d:
In San Marino, the documented reach into government comes from builders and bankers who paid politicians for the permits and licences they needed. In a state of about 34,000 people, a small number of politicians decide who may build and who may open a bank, and the courts have found that those decisions were bought.

In the case known as Conto Mazzini, named after an account held under the name 'Giuseppe Mazzini' at a Sammarinese bank, prosecutors showed that construction and banking entrepreneurs paid politicians, including former government ministers, with cash drawn from that account. About 200 million euros were seized, and an appeal court upheld most convictions in 2022.

For residents, it meant building permits and banking licences went to those who paid, while builders and bankers who did not pay competed against firms that had bought their approvals, and the buildings and banks approved that way are still part of daily life. It also shows the courts reaching former ministers.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores San Marino in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

Serbia.d:
In Serbia the reach into the state comes mostly from Belgrade's organised crime groups, and they work through the security services. Gangs with a share of the Balkan heroin, cocaine and cannabis trade have recruited or merged with police and intelligence units, which gives them state identity cards, entry to protected buildings and warning of investigations. The clearest case came in 2003, when a commander of the interior ministry's special operations unit, which had fused with the Zemun clan, shot dead the elected prime minister, Zoran Đinđić. Since then prosecutors have charged a gang that carried state security identification and a businessman close to the ruling party whose cannabis farm, they say, was guarded by police and intelligence officers; both trials are still open. A court has convicted a former deputy head of the organised-crime police of demanding the return of a seized car to an associate of that gang's leader.

The intelligence service has also been tied to Russia. In 2023 the US sanctioned the head of the Security Intelligence Agency (BIA), saying he helped Russia's activities in the region and supported a drug-trafficking network and illegal arms shipments; he resigned under Western pressure and became deputy prime minister the next year. Around the First World War, secret societies of army officers decided much of Serbian politics.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10, near the top of Europe, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 4.9. For people in Serbia that means the units meant to protect them have been used by gangs, once against the government they had voted for, and the agency that guards the country's secrets has been run by a man a foreign government accuses of helping Russia and drug traffickers.

Slovakia.d:
In Slovakia businessmen and their fixers are accused of reaching into the police, courts, prosecution service and prime minister's office, and the public has mostly learned of it from journalists and leaks rather than from a court. A wiretap file leaked in 2011 reportedly recorded executives of a large investment group discussing kickbacks on privatisations with ministers, which the group called fiction.

The clearest picture came after journalist Ján Kuciak and his fiancée were shot dead in 2018. Prime Minister Robert Fico resigned after mass protests, and messages on the phone of the businessman charged with ordering the murder showed judges and a deputy justice minister working for him. In 2020 police detained more than a dozen judges, among them the acting head of the Supreme Court. Prosecutors charged a former police president and the heads of the crime agency's top units with belonging to another businessman's criminal group; that trial continues. Not all of it has held up: the head of the office that prosecutes organised crime was convicted of taking a bribe to free an underworld boss, but the Supreme Court annulled that in 2025, and the former intelligence chief was acquitted.

Russian military intelligence, the GRU, works the same openings. A court convicted those in a chain running through a journalist to a parliamentary aide and an intelligence officer, to obtain the secret annual reports of Slovakia's spy agencies; police charged a former military academy vice-rector in 2022 with passing the GRU information.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 4.9. For Slovaks this has meant police chiefs accused of working for a businessman, court rulings that may have been bought, parliament's classified files reaching Moscow, and years of suspicion without a verdict.

South Africa.d:
South Africa's state has been run from inside by private networks twice in living memory, first a secret society and then a business family with foreign firms alongside it. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male society that placed its members in top posts; by the late 1970s it held almost every cabinet seat as well as the heads of the army and the intelligence service.

After apartheid the reach came through money. Foreign arms makers paid large commissions to win the 1999 arms deal, and under Jacob Zuma's presidency the Zondo Commission, a judicial inquiry, found that ministers and the heads of Eskom, the state power company, and Transnet, the state rail and ports company, acted corruptly for the Gupta brothers, Indian-born businessmen who offered cabinet posts to officials willing to cooperate. Foreign consultancies and engineering and software firms also paid officials at Eskom, Transnet and government departments to win contracts. A US aviation services company paid South African officials through an agent to win a component support contract with the state airline's maintenance arm, settling with US prosecutors in 2024. The same inquiry traced the pattern through other state bodies: money reaching staff of the state airline a month before a ground-handling contract, the family buying the armour supplier to the state arms firm Denel and then having its board replaced, the rail agency PRASA awarding billions to a shell company created for a foreign locomotive maker and to a supplier that had paid for its chief executive's homes, the public broadcaster carrying the costs of the family's television channel, and three Free State provincial contracts, one of them an asbestos audit that cost 255 million rand.

At Transnet the channel was advisory work: Regiments Capital and Trillian, linked to the family's fixer Salim Essa, were brought in without the required procurement to rewrite the business case for 1,064 locomotives, whose approved cost rose from R38.6bn to R54.5bn, and to run the swaps and the pension fund of retired rail staff. Today the reach also runs through the police, the prisons, local councils and public hospitals. Crime bosses have bought officers up to the national commissioner, and in Cape Town gang leaders have paid a police brigadier and got gun licences through staff of the police firearm registry. Supplier syndicates pay health officials to buy from them: at one Gauteng hospital investigators found more than R2 billion drained by suppliers working with at least 15 current and former officials, from clerks to senior managers.

For South Africans, the bribes paid to win power, rail and hospital contracts came out of the public money meant for electricity, transport and health care, and people who report gang crime cannot be sure whether the officer taking the statement, or the clerk issuing a gun licence, works for the gang.

St. Kitts and Nevis.d:
Nothing is documented yet for St Kitts and Nevis, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows an outside government, company, crime group or lodge paying Kittitian officials or placing people in office.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, places St Kitts and Nevis near the middle of its scale, at 5 out of 10. It gives about 5.4 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That describes officials under some pressure, with checks on them that are neither strong nor absent.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party. If outside money did reach in, it would most likely show up in who funds politicians, who wins public contracts and how licences are granted, and residents are best protected when those records are public.

Suriname.d:
In Suriname the cocaine trade did not need to buy officials from outside the government: for years it reached the presidency and the security services through the country's own leaders. Suriname lies on the Atlantic coast between Guyana and French Guiana, and the US Treasury says semi-submersible boats carry cocaine across the ocean from its ports and Guyana's.

Desi Bouterse, the former military ruler, was convicted in absentia in the Netherlands in 1999 of smuggling more than 450 kilograms of cocaine, never served the sentence because there was no extradition treaty, and was then elected president twice. While he held office his son Dino ran the country's counter-terrorism unit and used it to traffic cocaine; US agents arrested him in Panama, and he pleaded guilty in New York, including to offering a base in Suriname to people he believed were from Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed group.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.2. For the Surinamese, this meant that a counter-terrorism unit paid for by their taxes was used for drug trafficking, and that a court verdict against the man they twice elected president was never enforced.

Taiwan.d:
In Taiwan the main outside effort comes from China, through its intelligence services and united front work, the Chinese Communist Party's system for winning over or recruiting people abroad. A Chinese government office has paid for trips by elected village chiefs, and Chinese officials used the trips to urge them how to vote.
