Since at least the late 1990s Chinese intelligence has placed people inside Taiwan's state, and its main target now is the armed forces and coast guard. Investigators and courts have found agents in the presidential guard, military intelligence and the senior ranks, up to retired lieutenant general Kao An-kuo, jailed in 2025 for trying to build an armed group to help an invasion, which he denies. In 2024, 64 people were prosecuted for Chinese espionage, two in three of them serving or retired military.

Retired officers sign up former subordinates, loan sharks and pawn shops find officers in debt, and others are reached through temples, gangs, paid tours and a juggling association. Two journalists have been convicted or charged as go-betweens. Pay runs by the value of what is handed over: classified documents, missile data, or videos in uniform pledging to surrender. Not all of this succeeds: in one ring twelve people agreed and twelve refused, and courts have acquitted a former legislator and others.

Business money reaches Taiwan's own governments too. In 2026 a court found that a developer's bribes to Ko Wen-je as mayor of Taipei led the city to let it build far more; he can appeal. Foreign sellers have reached the forces as well. Over the six Lafayette-class frigates bought from France in 1991, a navy captain in the procurement directorate was convicted of taking bribes from the seller's agent, and the head of that directorate was found by an outside coroner to have been murdered in 1993 while gathering evidence of irregularities. France's financial prosecutor later found that Airbus's paid intermediaries had contacts inside the state-owned carrier China Airlines, including a board member, who passed out confidential information while it was negotiating an aircraft order. For Taiwanese voters this means the soldiers and aides meant to defend them against the government that claims their country have, in case after case, been working for it, and a city's building limits were raised for the developer who paid the mayor.

Timor-Leste.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Timor-Leste, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people inside its government.

Timor-Leste depends on oil and gas from the Timor Sea to fund its budget, and that kind of single, valuable source of public money is where outside interests often seek influence. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 4.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.9. That describes moderate pressure on officials with weak checks on them.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party. If a case exists, it would most likely surface through oil and gas deals, public contracts and policing, and those are the records residents would need to see.

Tunisia.d:
Tunisia's one documented case runs through a single border crossing. In 2025 a court jailed the head of a tuna and sardine export group together with the customs executive at the Dhehiba border post: the officer stamped the paperwork for shipments that never crossed, so the state's own records certified exports that did not exist. The export group needed only that one officer for its paperwork to pass as genuine.

Nothing else found so far shows a foreign state, company or crime group paying Tunisian officials. The best-known charge, that Ennahda, the Islamist party that led the government after 2011, ran a 'secret apparatus' inside state institutions, ended in a life sentence for party leader Rached Ghannouchi in June 2026, but Ennahda calls the charges political and rights groups called the trial part of a crackdown on opponents, so the map does not count it.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 6.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.3, which describes officials under real pressure with weak checks on them. For Tunisians, the proven instance is a border post certifying goods that did not leave the country, and it was proven in a Tunisian court; where else private money has bought an official signature is not on record.

Uganda.d:
In Uganda outside influence reaches the state through a foreign religious lobby working with legislators on its laws, through companies and brokers paying the men at the top for oil and arms deals, and through criminal groups hiring the police. The religious reach runs from the United States. Before Uganda passed the Anti-Homosexuality Act in 2023, Family Watch International, an Arizona-based Christian lobby that had coached African politicians for a decade, ran a private group of over 150 campaigners in which the Deputy Speaker said the ground was 'ripe' to bring the bill back; the lobby says it did not support the final version.

Money reaches the same level. A US jury convicted an agent of CEFC China Energy of arranging $500,000 for Uganda's foreign minister and urging a cash 'campaign donation' for President Yoweri Museveni so that both would steer business to the firm. Earlier, a judicial commission found that the president's brother took $800,000 from an arms broker over unfit helicopter gunships, and MPs in 2011 tabled documents alleging an oil company paid the prime minister and two ministers for its concessions, never tested in court. Lower down, the state's own force is hired out: in 2026 a court convicted four serving police constables of guarding a syndicate's fake-gold refinery, and prosecutors charged seven serving army and police officers with passing classified material to neighbouring Rwanda before dropping the charges.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at 3.7. For gay Ugandans, the effect is a law that can send them to prison for life, shaped with lobbyists from abroad. For everyone else, oil and arms deals have been settled by payments that surfaced only in commissions that led nowhere or in foreign courts.

United States.d:
In the United States the most common way outside interests get inside government is to write its laws and staff its offices. Industry-funded groups led by the American Legislative Exchange Council, where companies and legislators draft 'model bills', produced at least 10,000 bills in state legislatures between 2010 and 2018, more than 2,100 of which became law, and Christian nationalist groups supply bills the same way. A conservative lawyers' network supplied most of Trump's first-term appeals-court judges, and since 2025 many federal agencies have been run by people from the industries they regulate.

When it turns into bribery, it is a company buying the official who decides on it. In Ohio, FirstEnergy paid about $60 million to a group around the House Speaker for a law rescuing its nuclear plants, and millions more to the man who then chaired the state's utility regulator. Public purchasing works the same way: US courts have convicted contractors and suppliers along with the officials they paid in city public works departments, the United Nations purchasing division, the World Bank staff who pick who wins loan-funded work, and the football bodies that sell tournament rights. In each, the public's buyer was on the seller's payroll.

Foreign intelligence services, most often China's, recruit people in the State Department, the CIA, the FBI and the armed forces. Political movements have got in too: in at least four states, activists disputing the 2020 election got at county voting equipment, often with local officials' help.

For Americans this means Ohio electricity prices set by a law that was bought and a regulator who was paid, contracts and aid money handed out by officials the winners were paying, and in some counties election officials who let people set on overturning the result handle the machines that count the vote.

Vatican City.d:
The Vatican is both the centre of the Catholic Church and a sovereign state, with its own bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), and its own courts that answer to the Pope. Outsiders have reached it in two ways: financiers tied to organised crime and secret lodges who were given control of its money, and Cold War intelligence services that placed informants among the clergy around the Pope.

The money route opened in 1969, when the Holy See made Michele Sindona, a Sicilian banker who laundered heroin money for Mafia families, its financial adviser, and large sums moved from his banks through the Vatican to Swiss accounts. Sindona belonged to P2, a secret Masonic lodge that had enrolled Italian intelligence chiefs and politicians, as did the chairman of Banco Ambrosiano, the Milan bank whose collapse in 1982 still shapes how the Vatican is seen. The IOR was Ambrosiano's main shareholder and was tied to the offshore companies that held the missing money; it paid creditors $224 million while denying liability, and when Milan magistrates sought to arrest its president in 1987, Italy's top court ruled that the Lateran Treaty shielded him, so he was never tried.

On the intelligence side, communist Poland's secret police had an informant among the priests who looked after Polish pilgrims close to John Paul II during the 1980s.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10. For Catholics who give money to the Church, and for savers at the banks it deals with, this means losses caused through the IOR can fall outside the reach of ordinary courts, and any case against Vatican officials is heard by judges the Pope appoints.

Zambia.d:
What the record holds for Zambia is one contested allegation, about timber. In its 2019 report 'The Mukula Cartel', the Environmental Investigation Agency said traffickers supplying China with mukula, a protected rosewood, used the state forestry company as cover and shared profits with people around President Edgar Lungu, including his daughter and two ministers. It estimated that more than 50 containers a month left illegally over two years, with about $7.5 million a year paid in bribes and informal fees. The government denied the report, and the daughter and both ministers sued the agency in 2021, though she later withdrew. No court finding against them appears in the record, and Transparency International Zambia says most prosecutions are still ongoing.

If the report is right, protected timber left Zambia illegally with the help of people in government, using a state company as cover, which has not been proven.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Zambia in its Moderate band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 6.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.7. Beyond this one report, no case is documented of a foreign state, company or crime group placing people inside the Zambian government, so what is shown here rests on those scores and a disputed account.

Andorra.d:
Andorra is a small mountain state between France and Spain whose economy has long relied on private banking for foreign clients. That makes its banks the obvious place for outside money to try to get in, and the documented pattern here is crime-group money handled by bank insiders rather than by politicians.

The case on the map is Banca Privada d'Andorra, whose senior managers, the US Treasury found in 2015, knowingly moved money for professional launderers working for transnational criminal organisations. Andorra took the bank over the next day and wound it up within a week. The US later withdrew its finding, but an Andorran court sentenced eighteen of the bank's executives in 2025; they are appealing, and shareholders argue the bank was closed on an administrative finding never tested in court.

Outside banking there is little on record. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Andorra 1 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests, the lowest possible score, and 8 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, the cost of the bank case fell on its ordinary clients, who had to prove their money was legitimate before they could get it back, some waiting years, while the country's standing as a banking centre, which much of its income depends on, was put in question.

Armenia.d:
The cases on record in Armenia are accusations of spying for a foreign state, and most of them point to its neighbour and enemy, Azerbaijan. Since the 2020 war, in which Azerbaijan retook much of the territory around Nagorno-Karabakh, Armenia has opened several treason and spying cases against its own personnel. Investigators describe a former serviceman, reported to have commanded an army detachment, passing on troop deployments and commanders' names during the war. In 2022 the National Security Service said Azerbaijani operatives had posed as Armenian women on social media, befriended officers with access to state secrets and then offered them money; it said dozens of servicemen were involved and detained nineteen people.

In 2025 the accusations moved beyond the armed forces, when an unnamed Foreign Ministry employee was charged with treason for passing state secrets to a foreign state. Officials have not said which state and say no other ministry staff were implicated, and a newspaper's claim that the case involves Azerbaijan is unconfirmed. No case here shows an outside party placing people or money inside other ministries or companies.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Armenia 3.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 5.6 for its courts, police and watchdogs, around the middle of the range. For Armenians, the documented danger is that people passing on the positions of their own units, if the accusations hold, put soldiers and border villages at risk during and after a war. Elsewhere the scores suggest institutions that work moderately well, and the places to watch are who wins public contracts, who owns the companies running essential services and who funds political campaigns.

Bahamas.d:
The Bahamas lie on the sea and air routes between South America and Florida, and since the cocaine boom of the late 1970s traffickers moving drugs through the islands have paid the officials who police them. A Royal Commission of Inquiry reported in 1984 wide corruption in the cabinet and the police; it found that Prime Minister Lynden Pindling had received at least $57.3 million in cash and spent eight times his reported income, and five ministers resigned or were dismissed.

The pattern has returned, and it now covers the force at sea as well as the airports. A US indictment filed in November 2024 says that since at least 2021 two high-ranking police officers and a military official helped cocaine arriving on charter flights from Colombia and Venezuela pass through Bahamian airports and onto boats for Florida, for bribes of $10,000 to $2 million, and that one officer demanded $2 million on behalf of an unnamed senior politician; the police commissioner, who was not accused, resigned the following week. In 2025 a chief petty officer of the defence force was convicted of selling traffickers the positions of Bahamian patrol boats.

In 2026 prosecutors also charged a chief customs revenue officer over $56,320 paid by cheque by a contractor for services she had no lawful authority to give.

For Bahamians, forty years apart the officers guarding the islands' airports, coasts and customs desks have been accused of selling that protection, the biggest case was brought by a foreign court rather than their own, and the politician named as wanting a share has not been identified to them. The Global Organized Crime Index gives the country 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and 5.6 for its courts, police and watchdogs.

Belarus.d:
The documented cases in Belarus are few and all come from the state's own prosecutions, so they show only what the authorities have made public. They concern bribes paid to people running state bodies and state firms, and in two of the three the money came at least partly from Russian companies. A Belarusian court found that a Russian company paid a deputy state secretary of the Security Council, previously head of President Alexander Lukashenko's protection service, about $148,000 to promote its interests in the country, and jailed him for 12 years. The director of Beltelecom, the state telephone operator, admitted guilt in a bribery case whose charges included €15,000 from a Russian firm over equipment supplies.

The third case is in health. Officials allegedly took bribes of $10,000 to $450,000 from those seeking medical equipment and drug contracts, with prices inflated by up to 60%. Thirty-three people were held, among them a former deputy health minister and the head of the state medical importer, who was jailed for bribe-taking.

Lukashenko has ruled since 1994, and power is concentrated around the presidency and the security services. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Belarus 9 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3.1 for its courts, police and watchdogs. The KGB, the state security service, made the arrests in the health and Security Council cases, and no free press, independent court or opposition party can test them or say how far such payments go beyond these cases. For people in Belarus, this means public money for medicines and hospital equipment has gone partly on bribes, foreign firms have paid officials close to the president, and residents have no independent channel for raising it.

Bhutan.d:
Two cases in Bhutan meet the map's test, and both are suppliers paying the officials who decided what their firms would be paid for. In 2022 the Thimphu District Court sentenced the chief executive of Sai Trading Partner and a Senior Livestock Production Officer at the Ministry of Agriculture and Forests to three years and six months each: the company owner paid Nu 1 million for privileged information on a hatchery project at Samrang, passed the officer equipment specifications he had obtained from a foreign company, and the officer then made sure the tender document matched them. The officer said the money was repayment of a loan, and both men appealed.

In the other, Bhutan's Anti-Corruption Commission found in 2019 that an engineer and a procurement officer at Thimphu Thromde, the capital's municipal administration, had allegedly colluded with Bhutan Bitumen Industries: on an order of 75 barrels of bitumen emulsion the company was to keep 25 back and deposit Nu 75,000 into the officials' accounts, and the officials verified and paid for all 75. The Commission found the deposit was made, and charges followed against the two officials and three company officials.

Bhutan is a small Himalayan kingdom between India and China, and became a parliamentary democracy only in 2008. The Global Organized Crime Index gives it 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 4.7 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Both cases were found by Bhutan's own anti-corruption body.

Brazil.d:
Brazil has more documented cases of outsiders inside its institutions than almost any other country, and they come from three directions: organised crime, churches and business money.

Crime groups have bought police, judges and legislators for decades, and they now put their own people into elected office and into the workplaces they need. The PCC, a São Paulo prison gang that runs much of the drug trade, is accused of paying police for protection, financing candidates and placing allies in town halls around São Paulo, and has recruited ground staff at Guarulhos airport. Rio's militias, armed groups of off-duty police running protection rackets, and the Comando Vermelho drug faction are accused of having allies in the state assembly and Congress.

Churches reach in through seats and appointments: pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God founded the Republicanos party, which a church bishop leads and through which a bishop became a federal minister. Business money reaches state firms, the state's own lenders, lawmakers and the courts. Traders, shipbuilders and engineering groups have admitted or settled claims of paying Petrobras staff for contracts, and a meatpacking group settled claims that its money reached executives of the state development bank and a state pension fund, which then approved its financing and a merger. An airline paid officials to pass two laws cutting its taxes. The supplier of the counters that reported beverage production to the tax authority settled claims of paying a public agent over six years, in a case that began when the state mint's own presidency said employees were steering the retender back to it. Associations allegedly paid insiders at the pensions agency to take about R$6.3 billion from retired people.

For people living there, a bus fare or a tank of petrol can feed a crime group, a town's mayor may owe the seat to a faction, pensioners have allegedly had money taken from their payments with officials' help, and tax laws, public credit and state contracts have gone to those who paid for them.

Burundi.d:
In Burundi the documented reach comes from a foreign tobacco company working on the officials who write tobacco law. Leaked records from British American Tobacco (BAT), one of the world's largest cigarette makers, show payments to Burundian officials who handled tobacco control, part of a run of such payments in several East and Central African countries that researchers read as aimed at blocking laws modelled on the WHO tobacco treaty, which commits governments to restrict tobacco sales and marketing. A British fraud inquiry closed without charges and BAT denies the allegations, so these remain reports rather than findings.

If the payments worked as the records suggest, Burundians live under weaker tobacco rules than the treaty asks for: more advertising, cheaper and easier access, fewer health warnings, and over time more illness from smoking. No Burundian inquiry is recorded, so residents do not know which officials were paid or what they did in return.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Burundi among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest. On those terms, an official who takes money from a foreign company is unlikely to be investigated at home, which is why the only account of these payments came from a British broadcaster and a British university.

Canada.d:
Most of what reaches inside Canadian government comes from foreign states, as it has since a Soviet spy ring reaching into Parliament was exposed in 1945. China's reach now extends into state science: Canada's intelligence service has said a scientist at its highest-security pathogen laboratory worked to benefit China's government, and a researcher at Hydro-Québec, the provincial power company, is accused of passing its battery research to Chinese bodies through a Chinese state recruitment scheme, which he denies.

In politics China and India are the most active, working through proxies. Canada's public inquiry into foreign interference found intelligence that India's proxy agents may have given illicit money to politicians to elect pro-India candidates, and a parliamentary intelligence committee reported that some MPs and senators had knowingly or half-knowingly helped foreign states. For voters, a candidate on the ballot may have had a foreign government's help getting there, and publicly funded research can end up serving another state.

The other way in is construction money, aimed at whoever signs the contract. In Quebec, building firms rigged bids for city public works and paid both the Mafia and the parties that ran city hall; mayors of Montreal and Laval fell over it, and the country's largest engineering firm was convicted of buying a Montreal teaching hospital's own chief executive, who then shaped the tender so the firm won the building job. Organised crime also buys access at the border and the airport: officers at the busiest crossings into the United States have been convicted of waving smugglers through, and police say the ring behind a C$20 million gold theft at Toronto's airport had airline staff inside. Earlier, the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, placed its members in office: for decades every Toronto mayor belonged to it.

China.d:
Reaching-in runs several ways in China. The Communist Party places its own bodies inside companies, foreign ones included: any firm with three or more party members must set up a party organisation, and nearly three-quarters of private companies had one by 2018.

Businesses buy the officials meant to regulate them, lend to them or buy from them, and the record reaches the top: convictions for taking money from companies and smugglers have reached a Politburo member, the railway minister and the officials overseeing police, medicines and finance. State banks, which decide who gets credit, are a main route: in 2024 a central bank deputy governor and the chairman of Bank of China both received suspended death sentences for bribes from companies seeking loans. The same arrangement runs down into hospital purchasing, where a Dutch medical equipment maker settled a case over its China staff working with public hospital directors to write tender rules that only its own machines could meet. Gangs, for their part, have bought deputy police chiefs and village party secretaries.

Foreign spy services are reported to have reached deep into the state, though little of this can be checked. US officials told the New York Times that the CIA had recruited insiders deep in China's bureaucracy and that China killed at least a dozen of them from 2010 to 2012. China's Ministry of State Security regularly announces that foreign agencies recruited students and state employees, some of whom it says were executed, and the party answers with arrests and executions that no independent court has tested.

For people in China, this means loans, medicines, hospital equipment and trains overseen by officials who may have been paid by the firms involved, and no open way to judge who has really passed secrets abroad.

Congo, Rep..d:
The Republic of Congo's state runs on oil, and the documented reach-in comes through the circle around President Denis Sassou-Nguesso, who has ruled for most of the period since 1979. Foreign traders and oil companies have obtained the national oil company's crude and shares of the country's licences by dealing with his relatives and with intermediaries close to them, rather than through the state's own terms.

The clearest case is Gunvor, a Geneva oil trader, which between 2010 and 2012 lent the national oil company $750 million to be repaid in oil while paying nearly $30 million in commissions to two fixers close to the president's family; according to the case record the money was meant for his relatives, and a Swiss court convicted Gunvor in 2019. Norway's economic crime authority has since charged a unit of a Norwegian oil company over bribes it says were of particularly high value and linked to the president and his close family, after which the company obtained a share of Congo's oil licences; that charge has not been tried.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country among those where officials most often work for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs. For Congolese, this means oil that belongs to the state has been sold and licensed on terms set between foreign firms and the president's relatives, both accounts came out of European prosecutions rather than their own courts, and little inside the country would check such dealings.

Cuba.d:
Cuba is a one-party state whose own intelligence and security services control most of public life, and both documented cases of outside reach involve organised crime getting to the people at the top.

Before the 1959 revolution the American Mafia, through its financier Meyer Lansky, had an arrangement with Fulgencio Batista: Lansky's associates ran Havana's casinos and racetracks and Batista took kickbacks. After his 1952 coup Batista made Lansky an adviser on gambling reform, and the law was changed to let any hotel worth $1 million host a casino. The arrangement ended with the revolution, when the casinos were looted and then nationalised.

The second case ran through the revolutionary state itself. In 1989 General Arnaldo Ochoa, and an Interior Ministry colonel who ran the state's hard-currency businesses were convicted of letting the Medellín cartel move cocaine to Florida through Cuban waters and airspace, and both were executed by firing squad. It showed that a Colombian cartel could reach senior officers inside a state that tightly controls its own territory, and that they used state channels to help it. The trial was held by military courts that Cubans have no independent way to check, so the public record of how far the network reached is the one the government chose to give.

For Cubans, both episodes meant that decisions about their country, from who ran the hotels to what crossed their coastline, were sold by people in power to criminal outsiders. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cuba's officials as relatively unlikely to work for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength. No more recent case on the map shows outsiders inside the Cuban government, though the closed nature of the state means little would be reported if one did.

Djibouti.d:
Djibouti's documented case is a foreign company paying the state's own officials for a state contract. Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, admitted paying about €2.1 million to high-ranking Djibouti officials to win a contract with Djibouti Telecom, the state-owned telephone company, as part of a US settlement covering bribery in several countries. The payment went to the people inside the state who decide which foreign supplier builds a national network, so the contract was settled by the bribe rather than by price or quality.

For Djiboutians, the telephone network they pay for was built under a contract won by bribing their officials, and they learned of it from a US settlement rather than from any process at home. The officials who took the money were not named in public, and no case against them in Djibouti is recorded.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Djibouti in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs. The Ericsson payments are the only case on record.

Egypt.d:
In Egypt the outside forces that have reached the top of the state have mostly come through the army and through creditors. In 1952 the Free Officers, a secret network of junior officers recruited inside the army, seized power and ended the monarchy, and the body that succeeded their ruling council, the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, still sits at the top of the Egyptian state. Since then the army has been the place where others try to get in: an armed Islamist group built a cell inside it that killed the president in 1981, and a member of two presidents' inner circles was a source for Israel's foreign intelligence service.

The other outside force that came close to the top is the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 that works to bring its members into power. In 2012 Mohamed Morsi won the presidency as the candidate of the Brotherhood's own party; the army removed him in 2013, most of the movement's leaders were jailed, and membership alone can now bring a prison sentence.

Creditors set the older pattern. Sellers have paid their way to the legislature: Lockheed admitted in 1995 paying a million dollars to a member of the People's Assembly for her influence over the state's purchase of its transport aircraft, a sale paid for with American military aid. After Egypt fell behind on its loans in 1876, its European lenders placed their own commissioners over its finances, and the debt fund they ran lasted until 1940; from 1883 to 1907 a British controller from the banking family that held Egyptian debt, effectively ruled the country. For Egyptians the result is a state run by officers who arrived through a secret network, which treats an organised religious movement as an enemy within, and where people who voted for the Brotherhood saw their president removed by the army. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 8.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at 3.75.

Estonia.d:
Estonia is a NATO and EU member on Russia's border, and the most serious documented reach into its state is Russian intelligence recruiting people inside the institutions meant to keep its secrets. Over two decades Estonia has caught a series of Russian agents in its own defence and security bodies, paid by the SVR, Russia's foreign intelligence service, the GRU, its military intelligence, or the FSB, its security service. The clearest case is Herman Simm, who headed the defence ministry's security department, the office that protected NATO and EU classified material, and passed those secrets to the SVR for thirteen years until his arrest in 2008. The recruiting continues and now reaches lower: in 2025 a member of the Defence League, the volunteer force that forms part of national defence, was convicted of reporting to the FSB on fellow volunteers, soldiers and local politics in the border city of Narva. Estonia also convicted its first spy for China in 2021.

The second route runs through the banks, which money from Russia and the former Soviet states has used as a gateway into the EU. In the Azerbaijani Laundromat, about $2.9 billion moved in 2012–2014 through accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch, and part of it reached European politicians who defended Azerbaijan in the Council of Europe, Europe's main human rights body.

For Estonians this means that people trusted with state secrets, and neighbours in their own volunteer defence units, have been working for the power those secrets are guarded against, and that their banks were used to pay politicians elsewhere to speak for a foreign ruling family. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Estonian officials acting for criminal interests at 2 out of 10 and its courts and watchdogs above 8, and the spy cases have ended in convictions.

Finland.d:
Finland today has one of the cleanest records on the map. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 1.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts and watchdogs at over 8.4, among the highest in the world, and no current case shows a foreign state, company or criminal group paying Finnish officials.

During the Cold War it was different. The Soviet KGB assigned its officers in Helsinki, working under diplomatic cover at the Soviet embassy, to individual Finnish politicians and officials, so that many of them had a personal Soviet contact known as a 'kotiryssä', or 'home Russian'. The system reached President Urho Kekkonen, and a former Soviet diplomat later said the KGB general who ran it backed a candidate to succeed him. It is tied to what became known as Finlandization, the bending of Finnish policy to Moscow's wishes, and a leading Finnish newspaper reported in 2015 that the practice had almost ended.

What is documented now is the reach of a private elite network. The World Economic Forum, the Swiss foundation behind the annual Davos meeting, picks rising politicians under about 40 for its Young Global Leaders network, which brings them together with business executives over several years. President Alexander Stubb joined in 2009 and lists it on his official CV, and former prime minister Sanna Marin is also listed. Membership is lawful and public, and no finding says the network directed Finnish decisions.

For Finns, this means the foreign power that once had a contact for each senior politician has largely lost that access, and the open question now is whose views leaders hear in private meetings funded by large companies.

Georgia.d:
In Georgia, criminal and armed groups reached inside the state in the years after independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia has kept trying to recruit people inside its armed forces and diplomatic service, and the newest case reaches the security service. In the early 1990s a militia, the Mkhedrioni, was made the country's interior forces and was accused of extortion and drug smuggling until it was outlawed in 1995. Alongside it worked the 'thieves in law', a criminal fraternity born in Soviet prison camps, which 1990s governments treated as part of the power structure, Georgian analysts say. Membership became a crime in 2005, but police arrested more than 100 people in a crackdown in late 2025 and early 2026.

Russia's approaches centre on the 2008 war. A former counsellor at Georgia's mission to NATO was sentenced to 20 years, after a closed trial, for reporting arms purchases and troop movements to Russia; he denied it and said his confession was forced. In 2010 Georgia arrested air force pilots and a naval radio operator accused of giving Russian military intelligence its codes and readiness. Scam call centres, which phone people abroad and talk them into fake investments, have operated from Tbilisi, and in December 2025 prosecutors charged the State Security Service's chief from 2020 to 2025, a ruling-party member, with taking about $1.4 million in bribes, partly for protecting such centres. It is untried.

For Georgians this means armed men accused of extortion were once the state's interior forces, the army facing a neighbour that occupies part of their land is accused of holding that neighbour's informants, and the agency meant to protect them is accused of being paid to protect fraudsters. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 4 out of 10.

Grenada.d:
Grenada has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen, and the documented allegations here come from foreign investors dealing directly with the prime minister's office. In 2019 an Al Jazeera investigation reported that one foreign investor said he had paid about half a million dollars to Prime Minister Keith Mitchell, who said he received only $15,000 to cover travel. A US businessman said a partner had been offered a diplomatic post in return for kickbacks on state projects, which the government denies. No charge has been brought, and the claims rest on the investors' own statements.

For Grenadians, this means public contracts and diplomatic posts can be traded with foreign investors, and only the government's word stands between residents and that trade. If a kickback was asked for, it raised the cost of work done for the public. With no court test, residents are left with conflicting accounts. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 3.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.2, better than most of the region.

Guyana.d:
Guyana produces gold in its interior and has become a route for cocaine moving from South America by air and sea, and the people in both trades pay officials to keep their business moving. According to the US Treasury, the largest gold trading family in the country bribed customs officials to leave more than 10,000 kilograms of gold off customs declarations, paid officials for help in court matters and to win state contracts, and was helped by the top civil servant at the home affairs ministry, who took cash and gifts for contracts, gun permits and passports. The family denies wrongdoing.

Cocaine networks reach the police in the same way. In 2025 the Treasury sanctioned a serving police officer it says arranged safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers, along with trafficking bosses and Colombians managing hidden jungle airstrips. None of these cases has been tried, and the US State Department calls corruption in Guyana a significant obstacle to stopping drugs.

Outside interests choosing who governs is older than the drug trade. Before independence the CIA secretly paid opposition parties to remove the elected premier Cheddi Jagan, and kept funding their leader Forbes Burnham, who became the first prime minister of independent Guyana in 1966.

For Guyanese, this means the customs officer, court official or ministry clerk they deal with for a permit or passport may have been paid by a large private business, and duty lost on undeclared gold, more than $50 million by the Treasury's count, was public money. People in the interior live near airstrips used for cocaine, policed by a force that traffickers have reached. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 4.3.

Iceland.d:
One case in Iceland meets the map's test, and it is an allegation under investigation rather than a finding. Lúðvík Kristinsson, a traffic warden with the Reykjavík Metropolitan Police, was relieved of duty and Iceland's state prosecutor examined evidence that he carried out paid private surveillance while on police duty between September and December 2012, logging about 60 hours of it. RÚV's investigative programme Kveikur reported that the billionaire Björgólfur Thor Björgólfsson allegedly financed the surveillance through PPPSF, a security firm founded by two former police officers. Those watched were former Landsbanki shareholders behind a class action over the bank's 2008 collapse.

The Global Organized Crime Index puts Iceland among the lowest anywhere for officials working for criminal interests and near the top for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. On that estimate, an official serving an outside interest would be both unusual and likely to be examined.

The single case fits that: not a foreign state or a crime group, but a private litigant alleged to have reached a serving police officer through a security firm, and reported by the national broadcaster.

Iraq.d:
Since 2003 Iran's reach has been written into the Iraqi state, from the security forces to the cabinet and now the town halls. Badr, a militia formed in Iran in 1982, held the Interior Ministry, which runs the police. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), about 67 mostly Shia militias almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, were made a branch of the armed forces by a 2016 law and are paid from the state budget; their own chief of staff has said they take orders from Iran's supreme leader. The PMF has its own state company to win public contracts, and Iran-aligned armed groups hold ministries, including Badr and Kataib Hezbollah nominees in the cabinet formed in May 2026.

The militias also use their state seats and state-paid units to take over local government. The political arm of one PMF brigade won all four provincial council seats reserved for Christians by mobilising mostly Shia Arab voters, then used its majority on the Nineveh council to remove 15 mayors and directors in Christian and Yazidi towns. In Baghdad in 2025, gunmen from Kataib Hezbollah's state brigades raided an agriculture office to keep their ally in charge, and three people were killed.

Money flows the same way: about $2.5 billion was taken from a tax account through fake refunds, with the director of the prime minister's office among those convicted.

Foreign suppliers have paid their way into the security ministries too. In 2012 the officer heading the Interior Ministry's bomb squad department was jailed for four years for taking a bribe from the British makers of hand-held wands sold as explosive detectors. The wands have no working detection mechanism, and Iraq spent close to 60 million dollars putting them on its checkpoints.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Iraq 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3 for its courts and watchdogs. For Iraqis this means their taxes pay militias that follow a foreign cleric, those militias run ministries, a state company and local councils, and Christian and Yazidi towns can have their officials removed by an armed group's party.

Jamaica.d:
In Jamaica the documented reaching-in comes from two directions: money from a company doing business with the state, and criminal groups buying police officers.

In 2006 the oil trader Trafigura, which lifted oil for the Jamaican government, paid $31 million into an account linked to the governing party. The party called it a donation and said it was returned, and Dutch prosecutors investigated the payment as possible bribery of officials. The concern in a case like this is that a firm paid the people in charge of the government it was earning from, so that decisions on its business could go its way.

The second route is the police. In 2025 four detectives of the force's firearms and narcotics division were charged under the Anti-Gang Act, accused of forging a document to free a trafficking suspect on behalf of a criminal organisation. The charges have not been tried.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Jamaica 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Jamaica this means a firm holding government oil business paid into an account tied to the party running that government, and that the officers who investigate gun and drug cases have included some accused of working for the other side. Two cases are too few to show how common either route is.

Kenya.d:
In Kenya the documented reach into the state comes from three directions: drug traffickers moving heroin through the port of Mombasa, armed groups and smugglers working the border with Somalia, and foreign companies seeking public contracts.

The traffickers have bought protection where they needed it. The Akasha brothers, who ran a Mombasa heroin business, admitted in a US court that they had paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police for two years to block their extradition, and none of those officials has been named or charged in Kenya. Along the Somali border the record is less firm. UN monitors reported that al-Shabaab, the Somali insurgency, paid security officials on both sides to help a 2018 car-bomb plot through, without naming any official. A rights group has accused army units fighting al-Shabaab in Somalia of sharing in a sugar and charcoal smuggling trade with the militants; the military denies it.

Company money has reached the bodies that run elections and exams. A British security printer and its owner were convicted in London of paying officials at Kenya's electoral commission and national exams council to win contracts for ballot papers and exam materials. A former commission chief charged in Kenya denies it, and the commission's chair was cleared by the anti-corruption body.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kenya 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests. For Kenyans this means the judges, prosecutors and police paid by traffickers have still not faced a court at home, and contracts to print their ballots and exam papers were won with bribes, as a British court found.

Kosovo.d:
Kosovo's record shows two ways outsiders have got inside its security services: a foreign government working through them, and a crime group accused of paying them. In 2018 Turkey's government had Kosovo's police and intelligence service seize six Turkish nationals it wanted and fly them to Ankara, without the knowledge of Kosovo's own prime minister. A Pristina court later jailed the former intelligence chief for abuse of office.

The second comes from northern Kosovo, where the United States says a crime group run by a Kosovo Serb businessman bribed Kosovar and Serbian officials to smuggle goods, money, drugs and weapons, and that politicians gave it protection in return for campaign support. In 2021 Washington sanctioned the businessman, a vice-president of the Belgrade-backed party Srpska Lista and a former police operations chief for the north. An earlier indictment accused the businessman and the party official of leading a group behind a Kosovo Serb politician's killing, which they denied; in 2024 a Pristina court convicted four others, two of them policemen. The US sanctions are a government finding and not a court verdict.

The Global Organized Crime Index does not score Kosovo separately; North Macedonia's figures, 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for courts and watchdogs, stand in for it here. For people in Kosovo this means the police and intelligence officers meant to protect them have acted for another government without their elected leaders being told, and in the north some officers are accused of serving the people who smuggle through it.

Latvia.d:
Latvia has been reached from outside in two ways: Russia's intelligence services recruiting inside its parliament, ministries and key companies, and private bank owners paying the official who supervised them. By January 2024 Latvian public media counted ten people found guilty of espionage in the country, and the cases run from the interior ministry to a railway employee who was jailed for sending videos of NATO supply trains to a contact in Moscow.

The recruiting has reached elected politicians over many years. Leaked emails published in 2024 show Tatjana Ždanoka, who represented Latvia in the European Parliament for twenty years, reporting to officers of the FSB, Russia's main security service, from at least 2004; a criminal case is open but she has not been convicted. Jānis Ādamsons, a former interior minister who sat on parliament's defence and anti-corruption committee, was convicted in 2023 of passing material on NATO units and on Latvia's own security service to the FSB through a former KGB officer.

Bank owners have reached the top of the regulator. In 2023 a court sentenced the former governor of the Bank of Latvia, who also sat on the European Central Bank's governing council, to six years for taking a bribe from a Riga bank's shareholders in return for help with the financial regulator.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Latvia 2.5 out of 10 for officials working for outside interests and above 7.5 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in Latvia, this means an MP on the committee overseeing their police and security service was passing information to the neighbouring power those services guard against, and the official meant to keep banks honest took money from a bank's owners. Courts here have caught such people, often years later.

Libya.d:
Libya is split between a government in Tripoli and Khalifa Haftar's forces in the east, and on both sides armed groups have become the state bodies meant to police them. Militias hold official status as security agencies while staying loyal to their own commanders: one holds the capital's only commercial airport and its prisons, and another was placed under the Presidential Council while its chief's associates took over the internal security agency and central bank transfers.

The same factions are now reported inside the institutions holding Libya's money. The Haftar family network is reported to have taken the chairmanship of one Benghazi bank and a board seat at another, so that bank credit served people close to it; to have had its own adviser running the National Oil Corporation, the state oil company, so that oil sales armed its forces; and to have had a state bank's $300 million deposit stand behind loans to one of its fixers. None of it rests on a court ruling.

Smuggling networks have their own people in coast guard units, ports and fuel distribution, so the officials who should stop fuel, migrants and drugs leaving are the ones moving them; The Sentry estimates that about $20 billion of subsidised fuel was diverted in 2022–24. Foreign companies pay for the same access: one was convicted over a payment to the family of the man then running the oil corporation, and France's financial prosecutor found that an aircraft maker won a twelve-plane order from the state airline in 2006 through intermediaries paid for their closeness to Gaddafi's chief of cabinet and to his son.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Libya 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 2 for its courts and watchdogs. For Libyans this means the airport, the prisons and the police in their district may answer to a militia commander, their oil revenue and banks are reported to pay for one side's war, and they fund a fuel subsidy resold abroad.

Madagascar.d:
Madagascar's documented outside reach runs through elections and through the buying of state contracts. In the 2018 presidential race, political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Russian private military company Wagner, worked with as many as eight candidates, offering cash or promises of money, according to the Russian outlet Proekt and the BBC; the winner denied being Russia's candidate and no evidence showed he took Russian money. This is the approach Prigozhin's network used across much of Africa: back several contenders, so that whoever wins may owe something.

The other documented case is smaller and shows how contracts are steered. Inspectors for the Global Fund, which pays for malaria and other health programmes, found that suppliers had rigged bids for malaria contracts in 2010 and concluded that the scheme required an official inside the government's support office for health projects to work with them.

Both met a state that the Global Organized Crime Index rates as highly exposed, with officials often serving criminal or outside interests and weak courts, police and watchdogs to check them. That weakness is why no Malagasy court or official inquiry has set out who took money in the election or what was promised in return. For Malagasy voters it means they chose a president in a race where a foreign network was paying or courting candidates, with no official record of which of the people they elected, if any, owe that network anything, and that money sent to treat malaria in their country was shared out in bids arranged with someone inside the office handling them.

Mali.d:
In Mali, those reaching into the state are mostly cocaine traffickers crossing the Sahara and the Sahel, the dry belt south of it and the armed groups protecting them. Where the routes cross desert airstrips and border posts, traffickers pay local officials and armed groups to let the cargo through, and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime has found that traffickers include members of the political elite. The clearest example is the 2009 'Air Cocaine' flight from Venezuela, unloaded at a northern desert strip under protection investigators traced to local officials and armed groups; no senior figure was convicted.

Armed groups have also had their own members in official posts. UN sanctions listings say an influential member of a pro-government armed group sat in the National Assembly for the president's party while coordinating an armed blockade of talks on the 2015 peace deal, and that a member of a rebel group became special adviser to the governor of Kidal and used the role to control regional aid projects and extort aid organisations. These findings are untested at trial.

The military government, which turned from France to Russia from 2021, presents foreign intelligence as the threat from inside. In August 2025 it arrested two generals and a French national, saying he acted for French intelligence to turn officers against it. France has not commented, and the charges have not been tested in an open court.

Not all of it is the drug trade. A French supplier of betting systems admitted to the financial prosecutor in Paris that it paid about 79,000 euros to the chief executive of PMU Mali, the state-owned tote three-quarters held by the government and overseen by the finance ministry, for a contract awarded in 2007 without competition; the prosecutor records that he had never worked for the company. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Mali's courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest in the world. For people in Mali this means traffickers and the officials who shelter them are rarely brought to court, aid meant for them in the north has passed through armed groups' hands, and those accused of working for a foreign power are judged by the government accusing them.

Mauritius.d:
Outsiders have reached into Mauritius in two ways on the record: foreign builders paying officials for public contracts, and a foreign financier getting close to the head of state while seeking a licence from the state.

The contract route runs through middlemen. The money passes through agents or consultants, so the official who decides the contract never appears on the company's books. The African Development Bank, which lends for infrastructure, found that a Danish power-plant builder had more likely than not paid members of the Mauritian administration in this way during the tenders for the state electricity company's Saint-Louis power station, and barred it from its projects for nearly two years. That is a lender's decision, not a court verdict, and it names no Mauritian official.

The second case reached the presidency. President Ameenah Gurib-Fakim was vice-chair of a charity run by an Angolan banker, Álvaro Sobrinho, and used its credit card for private spending while he was seeking a banking licence from the Mauritian financial regulator, which she asked to issue it. After a newspaper published her card statements in 2018 she repaid the money and resigned, and the government set up a commission of inquiry into her conduct.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate level of officials serving outside interests in Mauritius and rates its institutions in the middle range. For Mauritians this means part of the electricity they pay for comes from a station whose builder was found to have paid officials, and their head of state was spending a licence-seeker's money while pressing the regulator on his behalf. No official has been named in the power case, so people do not know whether those involved are still in the public service.

Monaco.d:
The cases that touch Monaco come from the international bodies and wealthy foreign residents who base themselves there. The principality hosts sports federations and some of the world's richest people, and the documented problems arise where their money meets the decisions made in Monaco.

The clearest case is World Athletics, the governing body of track and field, which has its headquarters in Monaco. Its former president, Lamine Diack, was convicted in France of taking money from Russian sports officials to delay doping cases against Russian athletes, so that suspected dopers could compete at the 2012 London Olympics. In the second case, Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns the AS Monaco football club, was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including a former public prosecutor; the case was closed after the courts ruled that the phone messages it rested on had been obtained unlawfully, so no court has decided whether officials were influenced.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds a fairly low level of officials serving outside interests in Monaco. For people there, the athletics case shows a body run from their city selling decisions to a foreign state, at the expense of athletes everywhere who competed clean. The Rybolovlev case leaves residents with no finding either way on whether a wealthy resident could buy favour from their prosecutors.

Mozambique.d:
Mozambique has been reached from outside by foreign lenders and contractors who paid its officials, by timber traders who are accused of doing the same, and by criminal gangs with police and justice staff on their side.

The clearest case is the 'hidden debts'. Foreign banks, including Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB, lent about 2 billion dollars to three state companies for fishing and maritime security projects under state guarantees kept from parliament and the International Monetary Fund. US prosecutors said hundreds of millions went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and Mozambican officials, the former finance minister was convicted in the United States, and Mozambique's constitutional council declared the loans void. The state airline shows the same route on a smaller scale: a foreign aircraft maker admitted bribes on a jet sale, and a Maputo court sentenced a former transport minister, whose defence planned to appeal.

In the northern forests the claims are weaker. Campaign group reports say Chinese timber traders pay officials to move wood to port, and traders told undercover investigators that two agriculture ministers helped them. The ministers deny it, the anti-corruption office found no shareholdings by Mozambicans, and no charges are reported from these claims. In Maputo the country's own criminal investigation chief has said justice staff take part in kidnappings for ransom.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials serving criminal interests to one of the highest degrees anywhere. For Mozambicans the hidden loans meant debt their parliament never approved; when they surfaced in 2016, the IMF and World Bank froze support, and one study estimated that two million people were pushed into poverty. Families whose relatives are abducted cannot be sure the police investigating are not working with the kidnappers.

Nepal.d:
The documented cases of outsiders getting inside Nepal's state come from crime networks, a foreign spy service and foreign companies, and they work through the politicians and officials who control the borders, customs, state purchases and the awarding of contracts.

Crime networks reach in through the same people who make and enforce the law. In the 1990s an MP who held ministerial posts was reported to work with D-Company, Dawood Ibrahim's Indian crime syndicate, and with Pakistan's ISI spy agency, in gun-running, forgery and sheltering fugitives, a claim never tested in court. The current case is a gold-smuggling network: Nepal's anti-graft commission charged 28 people in 2026, including the chief customs administrator at Kathmandu's international airport and a former Speaker of parliament, after seized gold was swapped out of the sealed customs warehouse.

Foreign firms selling to the state buy the officials who decide. A US aviation-services company admitted in 2024 that it had paid Nepali officials through intermediary companies to win the sale of two Airbus A330 jets to Nepal Airlines, the state airline. In 2025 a court convicted two successive chairmen of the Nepal Telecommunications Authority, the industry's own regulator, along with the foreign bidders who paid them, after the cheapest bidder was disqualified and a phone-tracking contract went to the consortium instead.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Nepal widely serving criminal or outside interests and rates its institutions as weak. For Nepali people this means smuggled goods can pass the country's main airport because the officers checking them, and politicians above them, are alleged to work for the smugglers, and that aircraft and surveillance equipment bought with public money were chosen by officials the sellers had paid.

Niger.d:
Niger lies on a Sahel route that the UN drugs office describes as a natural stopover for South American cocaine heading to Europe. Where a trafficking route crosses a thinly policed country, traffickers make use of local officials, whose vehicles and offices are less likely to be searched; the clearest example is a mayor caught in early 2022 with more than 200 kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle, with no outcome recorded since. Higher up, a researcher has reported that a cocaine-linked businessman known as 'Cherif Cocaine' funded the ruling party's campaigns and was protected by officials at the highest levels, though the claim is hard to document.

The defence ministry has gone further than taking a payment: investigators found it had given an arms dealer's company power of attorney, its own authority to sign, so the man selling the weapons could also approve and certify the deals on the state's behalf. That removes the step at which someone checks what is being bought and at what price.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Niger high for officials working for criminal interests and low for the strength of its courts and police. For people in Niger this means the official stopping a vehicle may be carrying the load himself, the ministry buying the army's weapons let the seller hold the pen, and there is little reason to expect a trial that shows who else was involved.

Oman.d:
The clearest documented reach into Oman's state came from Britain, and its effect is still felt: the sultan whom British officers helped put in power in 1970, Qaboos, ruled for half a century. At the time Oman's armed forces were under de facto British command. On 23 July 1970 the British commander briefed the Omani officers who carried out a palace coup in Salalah that removed Sultan Said bin Taimur and installed his son, who was then under house arrest and had been sent the plan on cassette tapes by British officials. Accounts based on British records say MI6, the Foreign Office and the Ministry of Defence planned it and the prime minister approved it; Britain denied involvement for forty years, saying its officers had acted on their own.

Nothing documented since then shows a foreign state, company, crime group or secret society with people or money inside Omani offices or firms. The Global Organized Crime Index places Oman in its moderate band, scoring it in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Read together, those scores suggest that outside interests have some room to reach officials and that the bodies which would expose them are of middling strength.

For Omanis, this means the ruling line they have lived under for most of the past five decades began with a decision made largely in London, by officers commanding their own army. Today they cannot see whether contracts go to favoured firms or whether crimes linked to officials go unpunished; published court records, audits and lists of who owns the companies doing business with the state would be the first places such a pattern would show.

Papua New Guinea.d:
In Papua New Guinea the longest documented reach into the state is by logging companies, and officials have been found to help them at many levels. A government inquiry led by Justice Thomas Barnett reported in 1989 that some companies paid politicians and leaders to log forests while ignoring the law, with corruption, fraud and incompetence across the industry. The forests minister of the time was found to hold a secret stake in a foreign timber group he gave a permit to, and he was convicted of misconduct by a tribunal in 1991. A second inquiry in 2013 found that farm leases covering more than five million hectares, over a tenth of the country, had been hijacked by developers and people with vested interests, with corruption at all levels. Nearly all the operations were run by foreign companies, according to the campaign group Global Witness, which reported no prosecutions by 2014.

Other outsiders have used similar routes. A former executive of the contractor running Australia's asylum centre on Manus Island has alleged that some of that money reached a businessman close to senior officials, which is denied and untested. Drug traffickers have also allegedly relied on police help: after a plane carrying 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed near Port Moresby in 2020, the police commissioner said there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary, yet the officers alleged to have helped were not charged.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores PNG among the highest in the world for officials working for criminal interests and low for its courts and police. For people in PNG, this means decisions on who logs their forests have been made by officials working with the companies concerned, and they have little reason to trust the police to police themselves.

Poland.d:
In Poland, the documented cases of outsiders getting their people inside the state come mostly from Russia, Belarus and China and are aimed at people who hold secrets or useful records; one more came from private brokers selling faster visas.

Russian recruitment inside Polish ministries has been coming to light for more than a decade. Courts have convicted a defence ministry officer as a source for the GRU, Russia's military intelligence, and a ministry employee working on energy projects and on reducing reliance on Russian gas. Those now accused, who have not been convicted, include a defence ministry employee who had worked there since the 1990s, a Territorial Defence Forces radio operator, and a Warsaw registry official said to have sent records that helped build false identities for Russian deep-cover officers. In 2024 a Warsaw judge who ruled on whether military and intelligence officers could see classified information fled to Belarus; officials say he worked for Russia, which has not been proven. Prosecutors say Chinese intelligence worked through a Huawei employee and a former Polish security officer to win access to government data systems; both deny it.

The visa affair ran through the foreign ministry. Brokers got their clients' names passed from the ministry to consulates for quick approval: the state audit office found that a deputy foreign minister forwarded lists of people 'third parties' wanted approved, and he has been charged with taking bribes, which he denies.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Poland in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests. For Poles, this means people handling military secrets, gas supplies and civil records have reported, or are accused of reporting, to Moscow, much of the evidence is heard behind closed doors, and a visa could depend on which broker an applicant paid.

Russia.d:
In the 1990s, after the Soviet Union ended, Russian crime groups took over enterprises through their own people and ties with managers. The named leader of the Tambov crime group became deputy president of St Petersburg's main fuel company, one of up to 100 enterprises the interior minister said the gang controlled, and crime groups took control of the largest carmaker's sales network through its managers.

Now the FSB, Russia's security service, is accused of being used to settle business fights: an American investor says a rival used connections inside it to have him arrested in a fight over a bank, and his conviction was later vacated. The same services reach into bodies meant to be independent: reports for the World Anti-Doping Agency found that the sports ministry and the FSB ran a system through the Moscow testing laboratory that hid doped athletes, protecting more than 1,000 competitors between 2011 and 2015. Foreign companies buy their way in through officials at state bodies: a US transport firm paid an official at the state's sole uranium exporter, and an Israeli drug maker, US prosecutors say, paid a high-ranking official to boost sales in health ministry auctions. In the regions, a gang operated for years under protection from local police and authorities, until its members murdered 12 people.

For Russians, a business can be lost through an arrest rather than a court case the owner could win, public money for medicines can follow a payment rather than the best offer, and in some regions the police have protected gangs rather than the people they threatened. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Russia one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests and low marks for its courts and watchdogs.

Sao Tome and Principe.d:
São Tomé and Príncipe is a small island state in the Gulf of Guinea that shares an offshore oil zone with Nigeria, and its one recorded case of outsiders reaching in comes from the race for those oil rights. ERHC, a small Houston oil company controlled from 2001 by a Nigerian businessman who was a major donor to Nigeria's ruling party, obtained unusually favourable terms, including the right to pick the best blocks without the usual fee. In 2005 São Tomé's attorney general reported that bidding in the shared zone showed serious procedural deficiencies and political manipulation and that ERHC may have made improper payments to government officials. The FBI raided ERHC's Houston offices in 2006, the company denied wrongdoing, and no charges were reported.

The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic relations with many states, is also present; that is lawful and not evidence of wrongdoing. The Global Organized Crime Index scores the country low for officials working for criminal or outside interests, though its courts, police and watchdogs are also rated below the middle of the scale, which means fewer bodies able to find outside pressure if it were there.

For people in São Tomé and Príncipe, this means the oil under their waters, potentially the country's largest source of income, was parcelled out in a process their own attorney general found manipulated, and no court has said who was paid. They are best protected when they can see who wins resource rights and public contracts and who owns the companies that hold them.

Seychelles.d:
Little has been proven about outsiders reaching into the Seychelles state, and what has been reported centres on the heroin that moves through the islands of the western Indian Ocean. People who use drugs, prison staff and former anti-narcotics officers interviewed for research published in 2021 described police who release dealers after a payment, resell seized drugs and protect some traffickers while pursuing their rivals, and they said corruption in the anti-narcotics bureau reaches high. A parliamentary committee separately found irregular payments of about US$6 million, involving the drug-enforcement agency and the financial intelligence unit, sent to offshore companies in Mauritius.

None of this has been tested in court: as of 2021 the Anti-Corruption Commission had no active case of drug-related corruption. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 4 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.4, both near the middle of the scale.

For residents this means the agencies they are told are fighting the drug trade are described as compromised by the people who work closest to them, while no court has yet said who was paid or by whom. In a 2017 survey by the Anti-Corruption Commission, more than four in five of the roughly 15,000 people who answered said corruption was very high.

Slovenia.d:
The documented attempts from outside to get inside Slovenia's state have come through two doors: arms buying, where a single contract is large and the details are kept from the public, and the office that prosecutes organised crime. In 2006 Patria, a Finnish state-owned arms maker, won a deal worth 278 million euros to supply 135 armoured vehicles, and the Finnish broadcaster YLE later alleged that bribes were paid partly aimed at Prime Minister Janez Janša. A Slovenian conviction of Janša was annulled by the Constitutional Court and the case lapsed; defendants in Finland were acquitted and one middleman was convicted in Austria. No court has a standing finding that Janša took money, and he denies it.

Organised crime has reached the prosecutors themselves. In 2021 police said an official who had worked for about five years in the Specialised State Prosecutor's Office, which handles organised crime, had photographed files on live investigations, including orders for house searches and covert surveillance, and passed them through her partner to the Slovenian cell of the Kavač clan, a Montenegrin cocaine-trafficking syndicate. Two of the cell's key members avoided arrest, and the official had passed every background check.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 6.5 out of 10, higher than most of its EU neighbours, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 6.2. For Slovenians this means an organised-crime investigation can reach the gang it targets before the police knock on the door, taxpayers paid for the country's largest arms purchase while a foreign broadcaster said it had been won with bribes, and voters have judged the prime minister at several elections since without a final answer from any court.

South Sudan.d:
South Sudan's state has taken armed men into its own command structure. In 2025 the commander of the Agwelek forces, an armed group, was made one of the army's deputy chiefs of defence and his fighters were folded into the ranks, so the group now sits inside the national army. An army does not absorb such a group without taking on its loyalties: the commander's own men are in uniform and his chain of command runs into the force.

Business does the rest with cash. Illegal logging firms are reported to have paid the army, the National Security Service, military intelligence and county officials, the same bodies they negotiated their timber deals with, so the services that would stop the trucks have a stake in them instead.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 9 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at about 2, among the worst in the world.

For South Sudanese this means the soldiers in their area may answer to a commander who brought his own militia into the army, the forests being cut near them are cut with the security services paid to allow it, and there are few courts, police units or watchdogs able to establish any of it or to act.

St. Lucia.d:
Nothing is documented here, so this is an estimate. No case has been found of foreign governments, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Lucia.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 3 out of 10, which is low, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.5, near the middle of the scale. The main risk in the eastern Caribbean is the cocaine route north from South America, which passes through these islands.

For residents, the absence of a documented case means there is no known instance of officials here being paid or placed from outside. It also means the estimate rests on the index's own assessment rather than on any investigation or court case in St Lucia, and it would change if a case came to light, most likely through the drug route.

Sweden.d:
In Sweden the reach into the state comes from two directions: criminal networks working through ordinary public administration, and foreign intelligence services recruiting people inside Sweden's own security agencies and its companies.

The criminal route is the larger one today. A 2023 research review for the SNS think tank found that criminal networks have people inside government agencies, run companies in the welfare sector, such as home care, schools and assistance services, and draw on social insurance; wrong welfare payments are estimated at 13 to 16 billion kronor a year. Municipalities are most exposed, as they spend much of the money with less oversight.
